The connection between a wrestler's absolute strength and his bodymass is expressed by another power law 
equation: log F * log 1.005 + 0.724 log B (Martirosov et al, 1967). A linear dependence between the strength of 
certain muscles and bodymass has also been observed in wrestlers.
Quantitative analysis has corroborated the close connection between bodymass and weightlifting 
achievements (Rasch, 1960; Starodubtscv, 1966; Pismyensky, 1974). However, this dependence is associated 
only with maximum strength and not the speed with which it is displayed. If speed is considered, then the 
relationship between bodymass and strength is totally different. The correlation between bodymass and the 
weight of the barbell decreases as the speed of the lift increases. It is 0.719 for the standing press, 0.706 for the 
dean-and-jerk and 0.685 for the snatch (Starodubtsev, 1966). A decrease in bodymass has a far smaller effect on 
the snatch than the press (Vorobyev, 1964; Medvedev & Tumanyan, 1967).
Thus, the highest correlation between muscle mass and strength is observed in those cases when strength is 
maximal and the speed at which it is displayed is of secondary significance. The correlation between strength and 
bodymass decreases as the speed at which strength is displayed increases, or to be more precise, a higher 
correlation is not vital for explosive types of activity, especially jumping exercises (Smith, 1961; Kuras, 1962; 
Schunkc & Peters, 1962).

3.4 Factors Increasing the Working Effect of Strength
The strength which one can display is not constant and depends strongly on the conditions preceding and 
accompanying the motor activities. Therefore, in competing with respect to distance, time, rivals and gravity, the 
greater an athlete's chances for victory, the better he knows how to fully and skillfully use the potential of the 
nervous and muscular systems.
3.4.1 The Warm-up and Pre-Activity Preparation
The warm-up serves to raise the body to the necessary work capacity. The warm-up comprises two types: 
general and specific. The purpose of the general warm-up  is to increase the functional potential of the body as a 
whole, whereas the purpose of the specific warm-up  is to establish the optimal relationship between the 
forthcoming movement and the activities of the central nervous system which are associated with that movement 
(Ozolin, 1949; Krestovnikov, 1951; Miller, 1951; Blank, 1955). The raising of the work capacity of the body via
162


=== PDF 174 (printed 163) ===
SUPERTRAINING
the warm-up is determined both by central nervous and muscular system changes. In fact, use of the term 
“warming up” is often highly misleading, because this type of pre-exercise or pre-competition activity may play 
an even more important role in preparing the nervous system for the major sporting activity which is about to 
follow. In many cases, little or no general physical “warming up” may be necessary, as is often the case in 
Olympic lifting or gymnastics, where the athletes rely primarily on the competitive exercises or variations of them 
to “warm up”. Similarly, most or all warming up is unnecessary for endurance athletes, like marathoners, simply 
because the event offers more than adequate specific warming up. Consequently, the term “warm up” should be 
replaced by a term such as “pre-activity preparation”, which may involve neural ‘priming’, actual warming up of 
physical tissues, and psychological readying.
Naturally, the special part of the warm-up preceding all types of strength work is of particular interest (see 
review by Thompson, 1958; Swegan & Jankosky, 1958; Grose, 1958; Sedgwick & Whalen, 1964).
It is known that a muscle contracts more rapidly and more intensely the higher its temperature within its safe 
physiological range (Beritov, 1947). The electrical activity of a muscle also increases with rising body temperature 
(Golenhofen & Goptert, 1958; Book & Golenhofen, 1959), and after stimulation, the period of the active state 
decreases (Hill, 1951; MacPherson & Wilkie, 1954). Increasing the temperature locally increases strength, as 
measured on a dynamometer (Robbins, 1942) and by the amount of time over which a muscle is able to maintain a 
given tension or execute a measured volume of work (Nukada, 1955). A hot shower increases isometric endurance 
(Nukada, 1955), as well as the speed of muscular contraction and endurance in cyclic work, by 7.5-9.0% 
(Assmusen & Boje, 1945; Miudo, 1946; Carlisle, 1956; DeVries, 1959).
On the other hand, cooling can decrease strength and lengthen contraction time. Muscles cooled to 18C have a 
woric capacity period that is 2-3 times shorter than normal (Tikhomirova, 1961; Fray & Smith, 1941). It is known 
that massage has no influence on endurance in cyclic exercises (Karpovich & Hale, 1956; DeVries, 1959), but 
increases the power of explosive work (Skubic & Hodgkins, 1957; Merlino, 1959).
However, maximal work capacity can be achieved only after a series of muscle contractions, the number and 
character of which are determined by the functional state of the body and the intensity of the subsequent work. 
Repetitive work as a form of warm-up increases speed of movement (Swegan & Janosky, 1958), although if this 
work is of moderate intensity, then it is not beneficial for strength production. An active warm-up which includes 
intense exercises is an effective means of successfully preparing for speed-strength exercises and explosive 
exercises, in particular (Hippie, 1956; Michacl et al, 1957; Pacheco, 1957).
Thus, it was found that women basketball players increased their jumps by 1.0-4.5 cm (Panaiotov, 1962) and 
long jumpers by up to 10 cm (Diachkov, 1961). The punching strength of boxers increased an average of 400-700 
Newtons, while their striking time decreased by 0.02-0.04 seconds. It is interesting that the rest period between 
strong, rapid punches shows no significant relationship to punching force (R = 0.40), whereas after a warm-up, 
there is a moderate correlation (R = 0.62) (Karabanov, 1966). It has often been noticed that a 100 m sprint or a 
4x100 m relay sprint enhances subsequent long jumps (Verkhoshansky, 1961).
Therefore, preliminary work which is similar to the subsequent work significantly diminishes the time taken 
to complete a given motor task. However, it chiefly enables the muscles to withstand a large load without injury 
and execute powerful, rapid contractions. The movements included in the warm-up should be appropriate for the 
special exercise, not only in their coordination pattern but also in the intensity of the neuromuscular activity. The 
latter circumstance is particularly important for speed-strength exercises. In other words, specificity of warm up , 
like specificity of training, is also important (see 1.3).
To examine the necessity for pre-exercise warming up, it is necessary to look at several important issues, 
including the type of activity, the duration of the activity, age, individual characteristics, injury history and 
general activity profile. An extensive summary of the literature on warming up was presented by Franks, as 
follows (Williams, 1983):
• Athletes in high intensity, short duration events such as weightlifting and shotputting can improve 
performance by warming up
• Vigorous warming up can decrease performance in endurance sports
• Athletes in endurance events or low intensity sports do not benefit much from warming up
• Direct warmups (using activities directly related or similar to that of the sport) of moderate intensity and 
duration before explosive sports enhances the performance of trained athletes, but not necessarily of 
untrained athletes
163


=== PDF 175 (printed 164) ===
SUPERTRAINING
• Indirect warm-ups (using activities not directly related to the sport, such as cycling and stretching) can often 
enhance performance if kept at an unstrcssful level
• Almost all studies which show warming up to be detrimental used untrained subjects who apparently cannot 
tolerate high-intensity warmups
• Strenuous, non-specific warmups can interfere with sports requiring motor skill
• The selection of a suitable warm-up depends on personal experimentation with different methods in training.
3.4.2 The After-Effect of Muscle Activity
It is known that, if a muscle is stimulated by a series of impulses, its activity slows down more after the last one 
than when it is stimulated by a single impulse. Any stimulus, whether momentary or not, leaves traces in the 
nervous system. The traces or after-effect phenomenon  persists for some time after stimulation ceases, which 
reveals the relative inertness of the nervous system and its great significance for motor activities (Pimenov, 1907, 
Pavlov, 1929, Orbeli, 1947). In physiology, this specific form of muscular facilitation (see PNF, Ch 7.2) is 
referred to as post-tetanic potentiation,  in particular when the preparatory stimulus is produced by maximal or 
activity or 4 4 tetanus” (e.g. Abbate, 2000; Brown & Euler, 1938;. Burke et al, 1970; Grange et al, 1993; Marsdcn el 
al, 1971; O'Leary et al, 1997; Palmer & Moore, 1989; Vandervoort, 1983). These phenomena and the processes of 
adaptation associated with them form the foundation for fitness development. They determine the continuing rise 
in fitness, despite periodic interruption in the training process (Matveyev, 1964; Mateev 1964; Zimkin, 1965).
Research into the after-effects of muscular activity is contradictory, particularly in Western literature. For 
instance, a statistically significant increase in the speed of an unloaded movement was found directly after the 
same movement was executed with a weight (Murray, 1959; Van Huss et al, 1962). Conversely, other research 
could not detect such an effect, despite subjective claims by the athletes that their movements felt quicker after 
using loads (Nofsinger, 1963; Nelson & Lamber, 1965). No increase in the vertical jump could be measured 
shortly after preceding resistive exercises (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965). Shot-put results even deteriorated after 
preliminary throws with a heavier shot (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).
The after-effect has been examined in more detail in Russian research. It has been noted that preliminary 
isometric tension has a positive effect on the subsequent dynamic work. Despite fatigue following isometric 
tension, the effectiveness of dynamic work increases, usually by up to 20% when compared with work executed 
without preliminary isometric tension. With the reverse sequence of work, results deteriorate (Shiedin & 
Kunevich, 1935; Vinogradov & Delov, 1938; Vereshchagin, 1956; Farfel, 1964; Uflyand, 1965).
The after-effect occurs immediately after preliminary isometric tension. The first dynamic contraction still 
retains some trace of inhibitory influence, but by the second contraction, strength increases sharply compared 
with its initial level (Leinik, 1951; Vinogradov, 1966). The data indicates that isometric tension under certain 
conditions can serve as a stimulus for dynamic work and play an important role in developing muscular strength.
Dynamic work with heavy weights (i.e. high tension with relatively few repetitions) also elicits a positive 
after-effect in the central nervous system (CNS), which produces a general toning influence on the motor 
apparatus and an improvement in speed and strength (Portnov, 1955; Ratov, 1957; Diachkov, 1961; Muravov 
& Tkachev, 1964; Letunov, 1965).
In practice, the after-effect phenomenon of strength work is used to exploit its immediate and delayed effects. 
It should be noted that there is an improvement in performance immediately following strong tension; i.e. this is 
an immediate after-effect. In addition, intense preliminary strength tension improves results in jumping exercises 
(Diachkov, 1958; 1961; Verkhoshansky, 1961; Tatian, 1964; Tkachev, 1967), in shotputting (Fritsch, 1961; 
Ivanova, 1964; Markov, 1966), and in rowing (Ermishkin & Vozniak, 1965; Chuprun, 1966).
For the delayed effects, preliminary stimulation is used to improve the functional state of the neuromuscular 
apparatus during the athlete's preparation for competition or in training for speed-strength (Diachkov, 1961; 
Vrzhesnevsky, 1964; Khodykin, 1976). The positive effect is obtained only if this state is promoted at an 
optimal level of stimulation. Over-excitation of the CNS has a negative effect on the precision and coordination of 
movements, i.e. on athletic skill (Diachkov, 1961; Yakimova, 1964).
The after-effect phenomenon in the nervous system and its influence on the subsequent work is influenced by 
many factors, in particular, the strength of the stimulus, fatigue and the time interval separating the preceding 
activity from the subsequent activity. Thus, after tonic work (with barbell squats) the following changes in the
164


=== PDF 176 (printed 165) ===
SUPERTRAINING
parameters of the force-time curve F(t) of explosive isometric force in a controlled task (leg extension), may be 
observed (Fig 3.27):
• maximum force increases significantly over the first minute, by 25% of the initial level
• after 4 to 5 minutes the force continues to grow to 65%.
The beginning region of the F(t) curve undergoes less significant change because the magnitude and duration exceed 
the initial levels by a smaller amount, the closer the beginning force is to the F(t) ordinate. The time required to 
reach maximum force was reduced by 2.6% immediately after tonic work and by 4.6% after 3-4 minutes (Fig 
328). Later it began to increase until it exceeded the initial level (Tatian, 1964).
figure 3.27 The force-time curve of explosive isometric effort achieved for leg extensions with different resistances FI .............Fmax at
various times after barbell squatting. The dashed lines indicate the starting values of the force (e.g. Fmax: s refers to the starting value 
for the curve Fmax and F2: s is the starting value for curve F2). (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Figure 3.28 Variation in time taken to produce maximum explosive isometric force at different times after preceding tonic work 
(Vcrkhoshansky. 1977).
For moderately qualified athletes, the largest increase (90%) in dynamic strength after a static effort corresponds 
to a load of 50% of 1  repetition maximum (1RM), while the smallest increases corresponded to loads of 25% of 
IRM (6.7%) and 100% of 1RM (5.8%). With increase in fitness, the post-work improvement can occur with 
large loads of up to 100% of maximum (Ilin, 1961). Consequently, with the rise in fitness and the strength of the 
stimulus, the ability to evoke a subsequent positive effect also rises. However, in principle, the optimal and not 
the maximal load is necessary for obtaining the greatest post-work improvement.
The strength of the stimulus also determines the time taken to achieve the maximum lifting force and the 
duration of the after-effect. Therefore, from a practical standpoint, the moment at which subsequent work begins 
is of some importance. For example, vertical jump height varied in the post-work period, depending on the nature 
of the tonic work (Fig 3.29). Three to four minutes after barbell squats the height of the jump was 6.8% above 
initial levels, and 8-10 minutes after depth jumps, it was 8.0% above initial levels (Tatian, 1964).
In experiments with preliminary isometric tension (Ilin, 1961), the maximum was achieved most rapidly with 
loads of 25% of IRM (after 12 minutes), and most slowly with 100% of IRM (after 15.4 minutes) and 50% of 
IRM (after 17.2 minutes). Research has determined that the optimal rest interval between sets in weightlifting 
(during the presence of the after-effect phenomenon in the CNS) is 2-5 minutes, with the rest period increasing 
with the bodymass of the lifter (Ermolayev, 1937; Krestovnikov, 1952; Budze, 1959; Kazakov, 1961). It has

of strength preparation via a more limited volume of training work. Athletes and coaches have great potential for

3.4.3 Additional Movement
Some experienced coaches judge the mastery of a sprinter by the action of his jaws. If the teeth are clenched and 
the face has a strained expression during a race, then the level of proficiency is regarded as low. If the jaw is 
relaxed and the face is calm, then their movements are fluid and unconstrained and the athlete displays the skill for 
running fast. Although subjective, it is a reasonably accurate evaluation of mastery in cyclic movements when the 
muscles work in a rapid sequence of tension and relaxation. Clinically, this observation would appear to relate, at 
least in part, to the TMJ (tempcro-mandibular joint) syndrome sometimes treated by physical therapists to 
relieve muscular stress in various parts of the body which are distant from the jaw.
However, in acyclic movements requiring the display of powerful force, it is not possible to evaluate 
proficiency in this way. In this case, muscular force is concentrated in a single instantaneous contraction and even 
the anatomical antagonists may function as synergists. Under these conditions, the so-called additional movement 
contributes to raising the working effect. In physiotherapeutic PNF (see 7.2), this phenomenon is regarded as a 
consequence of what is termed overflow  or irradiation  from stronger to weaker or more fatigued muscles (Knott &  
Voss, 1968).
Muscular activity (an indicator of electrical excitation) is dependent not only on the processes taking place 
within the prime movers, but also on the state of the other muscle groups. Both unloaded and loaded movements 
with large resistance elicit electrical activity in the unexercised musculature of the body (Farfel, 1961; Levin, 1964; 
Sills & Olson, 1958). Furthermore, the strength and endurance of the arm musclcs executing dynamic work 
increase significantly by including other skeletal muscles in the work (Gorbunova & Khabarova, 1955; 
Mukhamedova, 1958). Exercising the muscles on one side of the body causes an increase in strength on the 
unexercised side, i.e., the well-known 'cross training' phenomenon (Wissler & Richardson, 1900; Davis, 1942; 
Hellebrant et al, 1947; Laun, 1954; Enoka, 1988).
Thus, an additional movement which does not serve to increase the economy of the motor action, has a 
specific physiological value and its systematic involvement can be very useful.
The combination of two or several muscle groups involved simultaneously or sequentially offers several 
advantages. Thus, the amount of force developed by the right arm is significantly influenced by the muscles 
taking part in the additional movement: a momentary contraction of the extensors of the left elbow increases the 
strength and speed of the flexors of the right elbow to a larger degree than a contraction of the left elbow flexors 
(Mukhammedova, 1958). If, during rhythmic flexing of the right arm, the extensors of the left are momentarily
166

tensed, then the work capacity of the right arm will increase by 39-42%; if the flexors of the left arm are tensed, it 
will decrease by 8-22%. Tensing the extensors of the left arm after first fatiguing the flexors of the right, increases 
the capacity of the latter to do significantly more work. Tensing the flexors of the left arm has no effect in this 
case (Popov, 1938).
Thus, the change in the work capacity of one muscle group by recruiting others into the work depends on 
many factors and varies under different circumstances. The athlete's fitness, the type of muscular activity during 
the additional dynamic or static work, as well as a decrease or increase in the load and work rhythm all influence 
the working effect (Vinogradov, 1966). Thus, in the above-mentioned experiments by Mukhammedova, a large 
stimulatory effect is obtained when the additional effort of the left arm reaches 25-33% of that of the right arm.
Finally, results are determined by the functional state of the motor system. Research indicates that, to obtain 
a definite stimulatory effect, the appropriate motor centre in the brain should be in a state of stable excitation and 
reactiveness. The excitation of one neurocentre stimulates this process in the other motor centres, if the latter 
centres become significantly dominant.

# Precise Muscle-Action Terminology: Why "Isotonic" and "Isokinetic" Are Usually Wrong

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky argues most everyday strength-training terms are
technically imprecise. Concentric: proximal and distal muscle attachments move toward one
another. Eccentric: they move apart (not literally a "contraction," despite the common
name — the muscle is returning toward resting length under load). Isometric: attachments
don't move relative to each other (joint angle constant); more accurately called "static."
"Isotonic" (constant tension) is argued to be almost never actually true during real joint
movement, since tension changes with acceleration, deceleration, and reflex activation
throughout a range; European and Russian scientists prefer "auxotonic" (changing tension
and length) or "allodynamic" instead. "Isokinetic" (constant velocity) is also argued to
be physically impossible over a full range, since starting from and returning to rest
requires acceleration; isokinetic devices are more accurately "quasi-isokinetic," and
isokinetic-machine torque output is typically much lower than isometric torque at the same
joint angle. "Quasi-isometric" action is defined separately: the slow, near-static muscle
action seen in heavy, near-maximal resistance training performed anywhere across a joint's
range (not fixed at one angle like true isometrics), relevant to maximal strength,
hypertrophy, and active flexibility training rather than power or speed. (PDF pp. 60-64,
printed pp. 49-53.)

**Why it works** — Real joint movement always involves changing acceleration
(Newton's laws), so any term implying a truly constant mechanical variable throughout a
full range is describing an idealization, not the actual muscle physics; the more precise
terms track what is actually held constant and where.

**When to apply** — **Inference:** relevant when interpreting or reporting isokinetic
dynamometer data (if used by Athletic Medicine or research collaborators): understand that

# Estimating Strength Deficit by Comparing a Static-Start Jump to a Dip/Countermovement Jump

**What it is** — Strength deficit is defined as the gap between an athlete's maximum
voluntary strength in a given action and their absolute strength (Fmm), the involuntary
ceiling for that same action (see [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]). True Fmm
requires electrical stimulation, which is impractical and risky to test directly. As a
field proxy, the text proposes comparing a vertical jump from a static, knees-flexed start
(no countermovement) against a vertical jump preceded by a sudden dip (a countermovement
that recruits the stretch reflex and involuntary/reactive contribution). A small
difference between the two jumps suggests the athlete is already recruiting most of their
available force voluntarily, i.e. training should emphasize raw force/strength capacity;
a large difference suggests a bigger untapped reactive/neural reserve, i.e. training
should emphasize "shock" and ballistic (reactive) methods instead. (PDF p. 20, printed
p. 9; the explosive-strength-deficit formalism, Fmax vs. Fmm, is credited to Zatsiorsky,
1995, discussed further via the force-time curve in Ch3.)

of involuntary reflex potentiation that a static start cannot access; the size of the
resulting performance gap is a rough behavioral index of how much of the athlete's
reactive/neural potential is already expressed voluntarily versus still latent.

# Eight Types of Muscular Tension, Classified by How and How Fast Force Is Displayed

**What it is** — Beyond the basic mechanical regimes (isotonic, isometric, auxotonic,
isokinetic, quasi-isometric; already covered in Ch1, see
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]), Siff and Verkhoshansky classify the
*character* of muscular tension in sport into at least eight types, organized by how
quickly tension develops, its magnitude, duration, repetitions, and the muscle's
pre-working state: **tonic** (large, prolonged tension where speed of development doesn't
matter much, e.g. holding a pin in wrestling or a barbell overhead); **phasic** (cyclic,
rhythmic tension-relaxation, e.g. rowing, swimming, cycling, distance running); **phasic-tonic**
(switching between dynamic and stabilizing work within one skill, e.g. gymnastics,
judo, wrestling); **explosive-isometric** (large resistance overcome, force maximum reached
isometrically at the end of the movement, e.g. snatching or jerking a barbell, and the
brief eccentric-to-concentric transition in plyometrics); **explosive-ballistic** (small
relative resistance, force peaks early/mid-movement then the load coasts on inertia, e.g.
shotput, javelin, tennis serve); **explosive-reactive-ballistic** (same as ballistic but with
a sharp, pronounced preliminary stretch immediately before the concentric phase, e.g. some
throws, wrestling and volleyball actions); and two **speed types** — acyclic (a single quick
momentary contraction, e.g. a boxing punch) and cyclic (repeated actions at a fast tempo
where each cycle's working effect must be sustained, e.g. sprinting). (PDF pp. 136-140,
printed pp. 125-129, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work," Fig 3.1; explicitly credited as
Siff & Verkhoshansky's own convenience classification, not an exhaustive or definitive
taxonomy — "we do not pretend to have classified all the forms.")

**Why it works** — The authors argue this classification exists because a "universal
regime of muscular work to develop strength" doesn't exist: which regime dominates a
given sport skill depends jointly on the magnitude, duration, and speed of tension
required, so training method selection has to be matched to the specific tension-type a
skill actually demands, not to a generic notion of "strength" or "explosiveness."

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist when auditing whether a strength exercise
actually matches a sport skill's tension character, not just its general "explosiveness"
label. **Inference:** in football, a defensive lineman's initial punch at the snap is closer
to explosive-isometric/ballistic (large resistance from the opponent, force peaking near
the end of a short range), while a wide receiver's release-and-drive is closer to
speed-acyclic; treating both simply as "explosive strength" training misses that they call
for different tension emphases. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in the department's
programming is already organized on Bondarchuk's general-prep/specific-prep/specific-development/competitive
spectrum (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing week1-lecture.md p.36); this
tension-type classification is a complementary, finer-grained lens for judging *which*
tension character an exercise trains, on top of where it sits on that spectrum.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves call this "only for convenience," not a
rigorous or exhaustive taxonomy — several sport skills blend types within a single
movement (e.g. gymnastics phasic-tonic transitions), and forcing a skill into exactly one
category can be as misleading as ignoring the distinction altogether. Do not use this as a
testing framework; it has no associated measurement protocol in this section (the
reactivity coefficient and depth-jump test for reactive ability specifically are covered
separately, see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**Example** — A boxer's jab (speed-acyclic, near-zero resistance, pure quickness) versus a
heavy bag power punch after a slight lean-back (explosive-reactive-ballistic, preliminary
stretch feeding a ballistic strike) look superficially similar but sit in different cells
of this classification, implying different primary training levers (reaction/movement
time work for the jab; stretch-reflex/plyometric-style work for the power punch).

**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (the underlying mechanical
regimes this classification builds on); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]
(explosive-isometric tension's plyometric transition phase); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the force-time analysis that follows for explosive-type tensions).

# Eccentric Actions Produce More Force and Cost Less Energy Than Concentric, by Specific Cited Margins

**What it is** — Three related, separately-sourced findings on eccentric versus concentric
muscular work: (1) **Force**: a maximal overcoming (concentric) contraction produces
1.2-1.6x less force than the same muscle displays resisting a stretch (eccentric), per
Bethe (1929); cited examples of eccentric-over-concentric superiority are 22% for the
arms, 46.8% for the forearms, and 50% for the knee extensors. Semyonov's 1968 data on
untrained subjects gives maximal isometric knee-extensor force at 120° as 465 N versus 401
N concentric; combined-regime testing found the largest force (506 N) for slow eccentric
action following preliminary maximal isometric tension, and 453 N for eccentric following
preliminary concentric work. (2) **Energy cost**: eccentric work uses roughly half the
energy of concentric work, but only at slow movement velocities not exceeding 0.12 m/s
(Chauveau, 1904; corroborated by later work: Fenn 1924, Hartree & Hill 1928, Hill 1930,
Cattel 1983); the advantage does not extend to fast, powerful concentric-style movements.
(3) **Reflex mechanism**: the myotatic stretch reflex strengthens with the speed of the
stretch (Samoyloff & Kisseleff 1928; Foerster & Altenburg 1933; Lippold 1957), and better-trained
athletes use this reflex tension more precisely and efficiently during eccentric work
(Zakharyents, 1962). (PDF pp. 136-137, printed pp. 125-126, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work.")

**Why it works** — The author gives a partial mechanism for (1) and (3): the myotatic
stretch reflex adds reflexive muscular tension on top of the passive/mechanical resistance
of stretched tissue, and this stretch-driven force addition scales with stretch speed. For
(2), the text does not give a mechanistic explanation beyond citing the calorimetric/heat
studies; **Inference:** the lower metabolic cost of eccentric work is generally attributed
in modern exercise physiology to fewer cross-bridges cycling per unit of force produced
during forcible lengthening, but the book itself does not state this mechanism.

**When to apply** — Useful as a citable, quantified starting point for programming
eccentric-emphasis work (e.g. eccentric overload machines, tempo-eccentric lifting,
eccentric hamstring work) where the goal is either a large force stimulus at relatively
low metabolic/cardiovascular cost, or building the reflex-tension precision the text
associates with trained athletes. **Eric's baseline:** none of the corpus's testing or
programming documents specify eccentric-only protocols, so this is a gap this text could
inform if the department wants a citable rationale for adding eccentric-emphasis blocks.

**When NOT to apply** — All three numbers sets are single old studies (1929, 1968, 1904,
with corroborating work through 1983), largely on isolated joints or untrained subjects,
not independently re-validated within this ingest; treat the specific percentages (22%,
46.8%, 50%, the halved-energy figure) as illustrative orders of magnitude from that era's
methods, not as targets to program against directly. The energy-saving finding explicitly
does not apply above 0.12 m/s, so it cannot be used to justify eccentric training as
"more efficient" for fast, powerful, sport-relevant velocities.

**Example** — A coach citing "eccentric strength exceeds concentric by up to 50%" for
knee extensors should attribute it to Bethe (1929)/Semyonov (1968) specifically and note
it as a single-era estimate for that joint, not a universal strength-training constant.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (the elastic-energy
storage mechanism eccentric loading exploits); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]
(the same stretch-speed-dependent reflex potentiation, applied to plyometric training).

# Eight Types of Muscular Tension, Classified by How and How Fast Force Is Displayed

**What it is** — Beyond the basic mechanical regimes (isotonic, isometric, auxotonic,
isokinetic, quasi-isometric; already covered in Ch1, see
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]), Siff and Verkhoshansky classify the
*character* of muscular tension in sport into at least eight types, organized by how
quickly tension develops, its magnitude, duration, repetitions, and the muscle's
pre-working state: **tonic** (large, prolonged tension where speed of development doesn't
matter much, e.g. holding a pin in wrestling or a barbell overhead); **phasic** (cyclic,
rhythmic tension-relaxation, e.g. rowing, swimming, cycling, distance running); **phasic-tonic**
(switching between dynamic and stabilizing work within one skill, e.g. gymnastics,
judo, wrestling); **explosive-isometric** (large resistance overcome, force maximum reached
isometrically at the end of the movement, e.g. snatching or jerking a barbell, and the
brief eccentric-to-concentric transition in plyometrics); **explosive-ballistic** (small
relative resistance, force peaks early/mid-movement then the load coasts on inertia, e.g.
shotput, javelin, tennis serve); **explosive-reactive-ballistic** (same as ballistic but with
a sharp, pronounced preliminary stretch immediately before the concentric phase, e.g. some
throws, wrestling and volleyball actions); and two **speed types** — acyclic (a single quick
momentary contraction, e.g. a boxing punch) and cyclic (repeated actions at a fast tempo
where each cycle's working effect must be sustained, e.g. sprinting). (PDF pp. 136-140,
printed pp. 125-129, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work," Fig 3.1; explicitly credited as
Siff & Verkhoshansky's own convenience classification, not an exhaustive or definitive
taxonomy — "we do not pretend to have classified all the forms.")

**Why it works** — The authors argue this classification exists because a "universal
regime of muscular work to develop strength" doesn't exist: which regime dominates a
given sport skill depends jointly on the magnitude, duration, and speed of tension
required, so training method selection has to be matched to the specific tension-type a
skill actually demands, not to a generic notion of "strength" or "explosiveness."

**When to apply** — Use this as a checklist when auditing whether a strength exercise
actually matches a sport skill's tension character, not just its general "explosiveness"
label. **Inference:** in football, a defensive lineman's initial punch at the snap is closer
to explosive-isometric/ballistic (large resistance from the opponent, force peaking near
the end of a short range), while a wide receiver's release-and-drive is closer to
speed-acyclic; treating both simply as "explosive strength" training misses that they call
for different tension emphases. **Eric's baseline:** exercise selection in the department's
programming is already organized on Bondarchuk's general-prep/specific-prep/specific-development/competitive
spectrum (`method-baseline.md`, "Strength and power," citing week1-lecture.md p.36); this
tension-type classification is a complementary, finer-grained lens for judging *which*
tension character an exercise trains, on top of where it sits on that spectrum.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves call this "only for convenience," not a
rigorous or exhaustive taxonomy — several sport skills blend types within a single
movement (e.g. gymnastics phasic-tonic transitions), and forcing a skill into exactly one
category can be as misleading as ignoring the distinction altogether. Do not use this as a
testing framework; it has no associated measurement protocol in this section (the
reactivity coefficient and depth-jump test for reactive ability specifically are covered
separately, see [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]]).

**Example** — A boxer's jab (speed-acyclic, near-zero resistance, pure quickness) versus a
heavy bag power punch after a slight lean-back (explosive-reactive-ballistic, preliminary
stretch feeding a ballistic strike) look superficially similar but sit in different cells

time work for the jab; stretch-reflex/plyometric-style work for the power punch).

**Related** — [[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]] (the underlying mechanical
regimes this classification builds on); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]
(explosive-isometric tension's plyometric transition phase); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the force-time analysis that follows for explosive-type tensions).

# Explosive Force Decomposes into Four Largely Independent Abilities (So, SS, AS, Vo)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's factor-analysis research on the force-time F(t) curve of
explosive effort (dynamic and isometric, across a range of loads and joint tasks)
identifies four component abilities that combine to produce a movement's explosive
force: **absolute strength (So)** — the strength ceiling; **starting-strength (SS)** — the
ability to develop the greatest possible force at the very start of tension; **acceleration-strength
(AS)** — the ability to build force as rapidly as possible once contraction has begun; and
**absolute speed (Vo)** — average velocity of an unloaded movement. Correlations between the
gradient (rate) components are specific: explosive-strength/acceleration-strength gradients
correlate ~84% (16% specificity); explosive-strength/starting-strength gradients ~52% (48%
specificity); starting-strength/acceleration-strength gradients only ~27% (73% specificity).
As external resistance rises, the dominant contributor shifts along the sequence **Vo > SS
> AS > So**: with small resistance (up to ~40% of So), starting-strength and absolute speed
dominate; with large resistance (>60% of So), acceleration-strength and absolute strength
dominate, with starting-strength playing a supporting role. A discus-thrower factor-analysis
example (Table 3.2, thigh extension) shows the top-ranked factor shifting from starting-strength
at low resisting torque to absolute strength at high torque, with the internal ordering of
all six named factors reshuffling as torque increases. Absolute strength (So) is essentially
uncorrelated with, or mildly negatively related to, unloaded movement speed (Vo), but the
strength-speed correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance increases. (PDF pp.
140-144, printed pp. 129-133, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Figs 3.3-3.6, Table 3.2;
Verkhoshansky 1968-1980 and Masalgin 1980 EMG corroboration.)

**Why it works** — Masalgin's (1980) electromyographic work corroborates the factor split
by showing the neuromotor patterns, motor-unit recruitment, and motoneuron firing frequency
genuinely differ between the starting-strength and acceleration-strength phases of the F(t)
curve — they are not just two arbitrary segments of one continuous process but reflect
distinct neuromuscular mechanisms, with starting-strength linked to innate fast/slow fibre
ratio (Vuorimaa & Komi cited as "Vutasalo & Komi, 1978").

**When to apply** — Use this to choose the training zone (load/resistance range) that
actually targets the ability a given sport action needs, rather than training "explosiveness"
generically. Training directed at one component produces "very little or no effect" on the
others per this factor structure, and low-correlation pairs (SS-AS at 27%) mean starting-strength
work will not automatically carry over to acceleration-strength. The text also notes the
practical training-difficulty ordering: **AS and So are easier to improve than Vo and SS**
(the more genetically-constrained qualities). **Eric's baseline:** this sits underneath
the department's existing use of [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]]
(Ch1) — this Ch3 material supplies the quantified internal structure (four abilities, not
just "RFD vs max force") that could sharpen how force-plate RFD/impulse metrics
(mRSI, force-plate driver metrics per the HD ODSF framework) are interpreted for a given
athlete's load profile.

**When NOT to apply** — This factor structure was derived from specific lab tasks (leg
press, discus thigh-extension) with instrumented dynamometry, on athletes of a given era
and training background; the text notes "the relative importance of each factor... alter[s]
depending on the character and especially the emphasis of training," so the exact
correlation percentages (84%, 52%, 27%) should not be treated as fixed constants
transferable to every athlete or exercise untested. Confidence capped at supported: this is
single-researcher factor-analysis work, not independently replicated in the modern
literature available to this ingest.

**Example** — A lineman's punch (high external resistance, opponent mass) should be judged
mainly on acceleration-strength and absolute strength markers; a defensive back's first-step
reaction off a stimulus (low resistance, own bodymass only) should be judged mainly on
starting-strength and absolute speed markers — the same "explosiveness" label hides two
different training targets.

**Related** — [[principle--rate-of-force-development-as-independent-limiter]] (Ch1, the
general RFD-as-separate-limiter claim this quantifies); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, the CFmax/TFmax/Fmm ladder — a different decomposition of "strength," not the same
as this force-time factor structure); [[claim--strength-deficit-scales-with-resistance-fraction]]
(same Ch3.2.1 dataset, the Fmax/So deficit table).

# The Gap Between Absolute Strength and Achieved Force Widens as External Resistance Drops

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) quantifies how the "strength
deficit" — the gap between absolute strength (So) and the maximum dynamic force actually
achieved (Fmax) — changes with load: at 80% of So resistance, Fmax reaches 94.0% of So (a
6.0-point deficit, Fmax:So correlation 0.822); at 60%, Fmax reaches 82.7% (17.3-point
deficit, correlation 0.798); at 40%, Fmax reaches 64.4% (35.6-point deficit, correlation
0.657); at 20%, Fmax reaches only 47.7% (52.3-point deficit, correlation 0.316). In other
words, the lighter the load relative to an athlete's absolute strength, the smaller the
fraction of that absolute strength they actually realize, and the weaker the statistical
link between how strong someone tests (So) and how much force they produce in that lighter,
faster movement. (PDF p. 141, printed p. 130, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Table 3.1, Figs
3.3-3.4.)

**Why it works** — The curves for different loads are described as "precisely superimposed
upon each other at their beginning" (early F(t) curve, Fig 3.4) regardless of load, which
the author attributes to starting-strength being a resistance-independent neuromuscular
ability; as the movement continues past that initial shared segment, higher loads allow
more time for force to keep building toward So before the limb finishes accelerating,
while light loads are already moving (and thus limiting further force production) before
peak force is reached — hence the growing deficit at lower resistance.

**When to apply** — Use as a citable, quantified rationale for why maximal-strength testing
(1RM, isometric mid-thigh pull) does not directly predict performance in light, fast tasks,
and why light-load/unloaded-movement testing and heavy-load testing measure increasingly
different things as load drops. **Eric's baseline:** this directly supports the department's
existing testing-battery design logic of using multiple load conditions rather than a
single strength number — e.g., pairing 1RM/isometric strength testing with CMJ and sprint
testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment"; force-plate CMJ family per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`) — because this table gives the quantitative reason
a single heavy-load strength number correlates poorly (R=0.316 at 20% load) with light,
fast output.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) built from a
specific leg-press-style task; the four discrete resistance points (80/60/40/20% of So) are
not a continuous, generally-validated curve, and the exact correlation coefficients should
not be extrapolated to other joints, exercises, or populations without re-testing. It also
does not by itself tell a coach what to train — it describes the relationship, not a
training prescription.

**Example** — An athlete with an elite back-squat 1RM but an average CMJ is not necessarily
undertrained; per this table, low-load output (like an unloaded jump, effectively near the
0% end of this curve) is only weakly tied to absolute strength, so the more informative
diagnostic is a light-to-moderate-load force-velocity profile, not the 1RM alone.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (Ch1, the SJ-vs-CMJ
field proxy for the same Fmax-vs-Fmm strength-deficit concept, which this table's PDF-page
citation explicitly points forward to); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the four-ability decomposition underlying this same F(t) dataset).

# Explosive Force Decomposes into Four Largely Independent Abilities (So, SS, AS, Vo)

**What it is** — Verkhoshansky's factor-analysis research on the force-time F(t) curve of
explosive effort (dynamic and isometric, across a range of loads and joint tasks)
identifies four component abilities that combine to produce a movement's explosive
force: **absolute strength (So)** — the strength ceiling; **starting-strength (SS)** — the
ability to develop the greatest possible force at the very start of tension; **acceleration-strength
(AS)** — the ability to build force as rapidly as possible once contraction has begun; and
**absolute speed (Vo)** — average velocity of an unloaded movement. Correlations between the
gradient (rate) components are specific: explosive-strength/acceleration-strength gradients
correlate ~84% (16% specificity); explosive-strength/starting-strength gradients ~52% (48%
specificity); starting-strength/acceleration-strength gradients only ~27% (73% specificity).
As external resistance rises, the dominant contributor shifts along the sequence **Vo > SS
> AS > So**: with small resistance (up to ~40% of So), starting-strength and absolute speed
dominate; with large resistance (>60% of So), acceleration-strength and absolute strength
dominate, with starting-strength playing a supporting role. A discus-thrower factor-analysis
example (Table 3.2, thigh extension) shows the top-ranked factor shifting from starting-strength
at low resisting torque to absolute strength at high torque, with the internal ordering of
all six named factors reshuffling as torque increases. Absolute strength (So) is essentially
uncorrelated with, or mildly negatively related to, unloaded movement speed (Vo), but the
strength-speed correlation grows roughly linearly as external resistance increases. (PDF pp.
140-144, printed pp. 129-133, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Figs 3.3-3.6, Table 3.2;
Verkhoshansky 1968-1980 and Masalgin 1980 EMG corroboration.)

by showing the neuromotor patterns, motor-unit recruitment, and motoneuron firing frequency
genuinely differ between the starting-strength and acceleration-strength phases of the F(t)
curve — they are not just two arbitrary segments of one continuous process but reflect
distinct neuromuscular mechanisms, with starting-strength linked to innate fast/slow fibre
ratio (Vuorimaa & Komi cited as "Vutasalo & Komi, 1978").

practical training-difficulty ordering: **AS and So are easier to improve than Vo and SS**

literature available to this ingest.

# The Gap Between Absolute Strength and Achieved Force Widens as External Resistance Drops

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) quantifies how the "strength
deficit" — the gap between absolute strength (So) and the maximum dynamic force actually
achieved (Fmax) — changes with load: at 80% of So resistance, Fmax reaches 94.0% of So (a
6.0-point deficit, Fmax:So correlation 0.822); at 60%, Fmax reaches 82.7% (17.3-point
deficit, correlation 0.798); at 40%, Fmax reaches 64.4% (35.6-point deficit, correlation
0.657); at 20%, Fmax reaches only 47.7% (52.3-point deficit, correlation 0.316). In other
words, the lighter the load relative to an athlete's absolute strength, the smaller the
fraction of that absolute strength they actually realize, and the weaker the statistical
link between how strong someone tests (So) and how much force they produce in that lighter,
faster movement. (PDF p. 141, printed p. 130, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Table 3.1, Figs
3.3-3.4.)

upon each other at their beginning" (early F(t) curve, Fig 3.4) regardless of load, which
the author attributes to starting-strength being a resistance-independent neuromuscular
ability; as the movement continues past that initial shared segment, higher loads allow
more time for force to keep building toward So before the limb finishes accelerating,
while light loads are already moving (and thus limiting further force production) before
peak force is reached — hence the growing deficit at lower resistance.

(1RM, isometric mid-thigh pull) does not directly predict performance in light, fast tasks,

different things as load drops. **Eric's baseline:** this directly supports the department's

a single heavy-load strength number correlates poorly (R=0.316 at 20% load) with light,
fast output.

# Reaction Time Is Largely Fixed by Genetics; Movement Time Is What Training Actually Changes

**What it is** — "Quickness" (rapid CNS-driven muscle contraction/relaxation without
preliminary stretch, against negligible resistance) is measured as **reaction time**
(stimulus to response/movement-initiation) and is distinct from **movement time** (end of
the reaction phase to end of the movement); the text states no correlation has been
demonstrated between the two (Harbin et al, 1989). Average simple reaction times by
modality: 0.142 s auditory, 0.155 s tactile, 0.194 s visual (Harbin et al, 1989); fully
unpredictable visual signals push reaction time above 0.5 s (Fogel, 1963). Reaction time
splits into a latency phase (stimulus to first EMG activity) and a response phase (EMG
onset to motor action); Hanes & Schall (1996) attribute reaction-time variability to how
fast a monkey's neuronal firing rate reaches a fixed movement-triggering threshold, not to
nerve conduction velocity differences. The text states the **latency period is determined
largely by genetics and minimally affected by training**, so quickness improvement has to
come from the movement/response phase: the average simple unidirectional movement time
(0.3 s) can decrease by more than 50% in highly trained subjects. For complex tasks
requiring anticipation/decision-making (e.g. striking or catching a fast-moving object),
performance depends more on accurately anticipating trajectory than on raw reaction speed
alone. (PDF pp. 144-146, printed pp. 133-135, "Quickness and Reactive Ability.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is that latency reflects largely fixed
neural-transmission and central-processing constraints (peripheral sensory-to-CNS and
CNS-to-muscle conduction delays plus a genetically-set neuronal firing-rate threshold),
while movement time (coordination, precision, motor-unit recruitment efficiency once the
decision/signal has fired) is the part of the chain that skill practice and strength/rate-of-force-development
training can actually shorten.

**When to apply** — Use this distinction when interpreting or designing "reaction" drills:
a drill meant to improve true reaction time (auditory/visual go-signal to first movement)
has a hard genetic ceiling and should not be expected to show large gains; a drill meant to
improve movement time (how fast the athlete executes once triggered) is where real,
trainable adaptation is expected. **Inference:** for anticipation-heavy skills (reading a
quarterback's eyes, a running back's cut, a hitter's release point), training time is
better spent on perceptual/anticipation training than on isolated reaction-time drills,
per the text's own point that anticipation ability matters more than raw reaction speed in
these tasks.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific millisecond values (0.142/0.155/0.194 s, the 0.3 s
movement-time baseline, ">50%" trainable reduction) come from a single cited source
(Harbin et al, 1989) and general kinesiology-era research; they are reasonable
order-of-magnitude reference points, not individualized benchmarks, and should not be used
to grade a specific athlete's "trainability" against a fixed target. The claim of "no
correlation" between reaction time and movement time is a single citation, not
independently re-verified here.

**Example** — A cornerback whose backpedal-to-break time is slow should be assessed
separately on (a) how fast he identifies/reacts to the receiver's break (largely
fixed) versus (b) how fast he physically executes the hip-turn-and-drive once triggered
(trainable movement time) — conflating the two risks programming reaction drills to fix
what is actually a movement-time or technique problem.

**Related** — [[framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization]] (Ch1, the
anticipation/mental-rehearsal mechanism relevant to the complex-task anticipation point
here); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]] (the force-side complement to
this quickness/reaction-time discussion within the same 3.2.1 section).

# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**: the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two characteristics
of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the field-practical form
**RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time to reach it, m is
the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Verkhoshansky's own
"reactivity test" protocol: a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after
a depth-jump from 0.4 m, unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added; jump height
and support-period duration are recorded and plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The author's mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force; RC operationalizes "how much of
that stored-energy advantage shows up, relative to how much time and body/load mass it
took to produce peak force," which is why it tracks support-period time more tightly than
raw force output.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); this framework is
the direct historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g) versus modern
RSI = jump height / contact time), and the load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky) protocol using a specific
0.4 m depth-jump height and 10-40 kg external loading increments on a now-dated athlete
population; the precise correlation values (R=0.95, etc.) should not be assumed to hold for
a different depth, load range, or sport population without direct testing. It is also not a
plyometric-prescription framework by itself — it measures reactive ability, it does not
prescribe how to train it (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] for
that).

**Example** — Two athletes with identical CMJ height can have very different RC/RSI:
Verkhoshansky's data implies the athlete whose reactive ability holds up (or improves) as
external load increases from 0 to 40 kg is a different training case than one whose
reactive ability only shows up unloaded — the former likely has more absolute strength to
draw on, the latter is leaning more on relative strength/elasticity.

**Related** — [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] (Ch1, the plyometric
training method this test is designed to evaluate); [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]]
(Ch1, a related but distinct static-vs-countermovement jump comparison for a different
purpose, estimating strength deficit rather than reactive ability).

# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**: the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two characteristics
of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the field-practical form
**RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time to reach it, m is
the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Verkhoshansky's own
"reactivity test" protocol: a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after
a depth-jump from 0.4 m, unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added; jump height
and support-period duration are recorded and plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The author's mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force; RC operationalizes "how much of
that stored-energy advantage shows up, relative to how much time and body/load mass it
took to produce peak force," which is why it tracks support-period time more tightly than
raw force output.

**When to apply** — Use the RC formula's logic (peak force relative to time-to-peak and
system mass) as the conceptual ancestor of modern reactive strength index (RSI) metrics.
**Eric's baseline:** modified RSI (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing is already the department's
chosen daily-readiness marker on ForceDecks (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and
neuromuscular monitoring," citing `2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md`); this framework is
the direct historical/conceptual ancestor of that metric (RC = F/(t x m x g) versus modern
RSI = jump height / contact time), and the load-dependent strength-speed finding here
(absolute strength helps at heavy loads, hurts at light loads; relative strength does the
reverse) is a useful interpretive lens for reading an individual athlete's mRSI trend
alongside their absolute- and relative-strength testing numbers.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single-lab (Verkhoshansky) protocol using a specific
0.4 m depth-jump height and 10-40 kg external loading increments on a now-dated athlete
population; the precise correlation values (R=0.95, etc.) should not be assumed to hold for
a different depth, load range, or sport population without direct testing. It is also not a
plyometric-prescription framework by itself — it measures reactive ability, it does not
prescribe how to train it (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] for
that).

Verkhoshansky's data implies the athlete whose reactive ability holds up (or improves) as
external load increases from 0 to 40 kg is a different training case than one whose
reactive ability only shows up unloaded — the former likely has more absolute strength to
draw on, the latter is leaning more on relative strength/elasticity.

purpose, estimating strength deficit rather than reactive ability).

# The "Speed Barrier" Is a Genetic Ceiling, Not a Mysterious Neural Block

**What it is** — The classic idea of a "speed barrier" — a plateau caused by monotonous
maximal-effort repetition — is rejected: "research has not found convincing experimental
corroboration" for it. Instead, speed of movement is described as having "an upper limit
that is largely predetermined by genetics," so that the halt in a sprinter's improvement
reflects reaching their individual genetic speed ceiling, not hitting some neural barrier.
Supporting evidence cited: sprinters' propulsive muscles run up to 75% fast-twitch fibre
(Gollnick 1972; Thorstensson et al 1977) versus up to 90% slow-twitch in long-distance
runners (Costill 1973); nervous-system excitability level is independently linked to
individual speed (Gorozhanin 1977; Sultanov 1979; Ilin & Malchikov 1979; Tabachnik et al
1978); economical sprinting recovers roughly 60% of mechanical energy expended per cycle
elastically, with the rest replenished metabolically (Verkhoshansky, 1996, uncited
underlying data); and there is a high correlation (r=0.785) between a muscle's elastic
energy-storage capacity and distance-runner performance specifically. The text also notes
that some sprinters improve mainly via strength increases while their muscle-relaxation
ability stays constant, while other talented sprinters improve mainly via better muscle
relaxation efficiency — two distinct improvement pathways to the same outcome. Practical
implication stated directly: "the preparation of high-class sprinters is associated not so
much with the absolute development of speed as it is with the selection of genetically
gifted people and the efficient organisation of training." (PDF pp. 149-150, printed pp.
138-139, "Speed, Speed-Strength and Quickness.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is that speed of movement in cyclic locomotion
depends on complex, whole-system neurophysiological control (not simple, isolated-joint
speed qualities), and multiple independently-genetic factors (fibre-type ratio, CNS
excitability, elastic-energy-return efficiency) jointly cap how fast any one individual can
ultimately move — training can approach that ceiling efficiently, but cannot exceed the
combination of these genetically-set inputs.

**When to apply** — Use this to set realistic expectations for how much a given athlete's
top-end speed can change with training, and to justify individualizing the *pathway* to
speed improvement (strength-driven vs. relaxation/efficiency-driven) rather than assuming
one speed-training template fits all athletes. **Eric's baseline:** this aligns with and
gives a physiological rationale for the department's existing framing that "speed is
harder to train and more genetically constrained than strength or power" while still being
"the biggest separator between good and great athletes" (`method-baseline.md`, "Speed and
sprint," citing 01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.11).

**When NOT to apply** — The specific supporting numbers (75%/90% fibre-type extremes, the
60% elastic-energy-return figure, r=0.785) are drawn from a scattered set of older,
mostly single-study citations across different populations; they illustrate the range and
direction of the genetic-ceiling argument, not precise, individually-applicable targets.
This claim should not be used to argue speed is untrainable — the text explicitly says
training organization still matters for reaching one's genetic ceiling efficiently, only
that it cannot be trained past that ceiling.

**Example** — Two sprinters plateauing at the same 40-time should not automatically get the
same "break the barrier" intervention; per this framework, one may have room to improve via
added strength (if their relaxation efficiency is already good), the other via relaxation/coordination
work (if they are already strong relative to their speed), and testing which lever is
slack matters more than a generic max-velocity block for either.

**Related** — [[framework--sarcomere-vs-sarcoplasmic-hypertrophy]] (Ch1, fibre-type and
hypertrophy-type background); [[claim--velocity-and-contraction-specificity-asymmetric-transfer]]
(Ch1, velocity-specific training transfer, a related but distinct specificity claim).

# Strength-Endurance Splits Two Ways (Dynamic/Static, General/Local), and "Absolute" vs "Partial" Endurance Explains Contradictory Research

**What it is** — Strength-endurance (sustained muscle tension with minimal efficiency loss,
e.g. a rower averaging 40-60 kgf per stroke over 230-250 strokes in 6-7 minutes, Samsonov
1969) is classified along two independent axes. By muscular-work character: **dynamic
strength-endurance** (repeated tension without interruption in cyclic sports like running,
swimming, rowing, or repeated short-rest acyclic work like repeated jumps/throws) versus
**static strength-endurance** (sustained isometric tension or held posture, e.g. wrestling,
sailing, shooting, skating). By muscle-group involvement: **general strength-endurance**
(many muscle groups) versus **local strength-endurance** (individual muscle groups) — a
distinction the text calls significant for exercise selection, since training should target
the specific muscle groups actually driving the sport skill (demonstrated via EMG in rowing,
Lazarov 1967, and via strength-performance correlation in swimming, Shchavelyev 1969).
Separately, Zatsiorsky et al (1965) resolve contradictory strength-endurance research
(some studies found positive correlation with strength, some none, some negative) by
splitting endurance into **absolute endurance** (the overall result, ignoring the level of
underlying motor abilities) and **partial endurance** (the level of a specific motor ability
once the influence of other abilities is excluded, e.g. holding or moving a load at a fixed
*percentage* of one's own max, which typically shows no or negative correlation with max
strength, versus absolute endurance at a fixed *absolute* load, which correlates positively
with max strength). To compare partial endurance across athletes, relative (bodymass-adjusted)
static or dynamic strength-endurance must be calculated. (PDF pp. 153-155, printed pp.
142-144, "3.2.2 Strength-Endurance," Fig 3.12-3.13.)

**Why it works** — The absolute/partial distinction resolves the contradiction
mechanistically: an absolute-load endurance test is partly re-measuring maximal strength
(a stronger athlete simply has more headroom under any fixed absolute load), while a
relative-load (percentage-of-own-max) test removes that confound and isolates the
endurance-specific quality — which is why the same construct ("strength-endurance")
produces opposite-signed correlations with strength depending on which type was actually
tested.

**When to apply** — Use the absolute/partial distinction whenever comparing
strength-endurance findings (in this book or elsewhere) that seem contradictory: check
whether the test load was a fixed absolute weight or a fixed percentage of each athlete's
own max before concluding the results actually disagree. **Eric's baseline:** the
department's own testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment") already defaults
novices and most women's-sport testing to repetition-max protocols rather than 1RM; this
framework implies that comparing rep-max results *across* athletes as a proxy for
relative strength-endurance requires normalizing to each athlete's own max (partial
endurance), not comparing raw rep counts at a shared absolute load, if the goal is to
isolate the endurance quality itself rather than re-measuring who is stronger.

**When NOT to apply** — The text is explicit that "an objective, reliable means of
evaluating strength-endurance in sporting activity has not yet been devised" and that
"specialists frequently use inadequate tests" — this is a classification scheme for
thinking about strength-endurance clearly, not a validated measurement protocol. The
archer example (Fig 3.13) shows that as athletes become more skilled, the correlation
between strength-endurance and competitive results actually *decreases* (control of
muscular contraction matters more than raw endurance), so this taxonomy should not be
read as implying strength-endurance always predicts sport performance.

**Example** — A quarter-squat-hold endurance test at a fixed 100 kg for a whole roster
measures absolute strength-endurance (confounded with who is strongest); the same test
at 60% of each athlete's own back-squat max measures partial (dynamic/static)
strength-endurance and is the more isolated endurance metric.

**Related** — [[claim--continuous-vs-interval-circuit-training-for-concurrent-goals]] (Ch1,
adjacent programming content for endurance-strength concurrent goals).

(some studies found positive correlation with strength, some none, some negative) by

underlying motor abilities) and **partial endurance** (the level of a specific motor ability

mechanistically: an absolute-load endurance test is partly re-measuring maximal strength
(a stronger athlete simply has more headroom under any fixed absolute load), while a
relative-load (percentage-of-own-max) test removes that confound and isolates the

produces opposite-signed correlations with strength depending on which type was actually
tested.

own max before concluding the results actually disagree. **Eric's baseline:** the

# Muscle State Just Before a Movement Ranks Performance: Stretched > Contracted > Relaxed

**What it is** — The state of a muscle immediately before force production (relaxed,
isometrically tensioned, dynamically stretched, or "shock"-stretched by rapid braking of a
falling load) changes the working effect of the subsequent movement. In a vertical-jump
experiment (no arm swing), height attained rose across four pre-working conditions in
this order: static half-squat start 39.0 ± 6.0 cm; after a preliminary half-squat 44.2 ±
5.0 cm; after a 0.5 m depth-jump 48.6 ± 7.0 cm (Verkhoshansky, 1963, 1970). Separately,
under conditions of preliminary muscular tension, subjects executed movements 4% faster,
with reaction time roughly seven times faster than from a fully relaxed state; the ranked
order of preliminary muscle conditions for fastest reaction time and movement speed is
**stretched > contracted > relaxed** (Smith, 1964), and a motor reflex's latent period is
shorter when the muscle is lightly tensed for as little as 10 ms beforehand (Person, 1965).
The text explicitly qualifies the common coaching advice to "stay relaxed": preliminary
relaxation should be understood as relative to the specific movement — eliminating *spurious*
tension (muscles not contributing to the task) is valuable, but optimal preliminary tension
for brief, explosive movements is appropriate and necessary, provided its duration is kept
limited (prolonging it reduces dynamic force). (PDF pp. 155-157, printed pp. 144-146,
"3.3.1 The Influence of the Pre-Working State of the Muscles," Fig 3.14.)

**Why it works** — When muscles start relaxed, they are "not optimally ready to work" and
produce a smaller kinetic effect than their capability; preliminary tension (the
"anticipation tuner" of the neuromuscular system, per Bernstein) and preliminary stretch
both pre-load the neuromuscular system so less time/force is spent simply activating the
muscle before useful work begins, and a genuine stretch additionally banks elastic energy
recoverable during the subsequent contraction.

**When to apply** — Use this to justify why a small preparatory countermovement, brief
isometric pre-tension, or short approach/depth-jump stimulus before an explosive test or
lift outperforms a fully relaxed static start, and to caution against blanket "stay loose
and relaxed" coaching cues for brief, explosive actions specifically. **Inference:** for
Baylor's force-plate testing, this is consistent with running both a static-start (squat
jump) and a countermovement/depth-jump variant in the CMJ family (per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`), since the pre-working state itself is shown here to
be a first-order performance variable, not just methodological noise.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific jump-height numbers (39.0/44.2/48.6 cm) come from one
Verkhoshansky dataset and should not be treated as universal benchmarks; the "stay relaxed"
qualification applies specifically to *spurious* tension in muscles unrelated to the task —
it does not license generalized excess tension, and the text separately warns that
prolonging preliminary tension too long reduces dynamic force output, so there is an
optimal (not maximal) duration and magnitude of pre-tension.

**Example** — A vertical-jump test protocol that only records a static-squat-start jump
will systematically underestimate an athlete's explosive ceiling relative to a depth-jump
variant, per this ~25% height difference (39.0 to 48.6 cm) found here — the two are not
interchangeable measures of "jump ability."

**Related** — [[framework--reactivity-coefficient-and-depth-jump-test]] (the same
depth-jump stimulus used as a measurement tool rather than a performance-boosting
pre-working state); [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (Ch1, the
elastic-storage mechanism behind the stretched-state advantage).

# The Classic Hyperbolic Force-Velocity Curve Breaks Down Near Isometric, and Has Several Modeling Limits

**What it is** — Hill's classical force-velocity equation, (F+a)(V+b) = (Fo+a)b (a
hyperbola), was derived largely from isolated (in vitro) muscle. Perrine and Edgerton
(1978), using in vivo human measurement, found the curve is **not simply hyperbolic near
zero velocity**: instead of rising smoothly to an asymptote as velocity approaches zero,
force/torque takes a more parabolic shape and actually peaks at a certain *low* (non-zero)
velocity before dropping to a lower value under true isometric conditions (V=0) — i.e.
maximum torque is not produced isometrically. Above roughly 200 degrees/second, Hill's
hyperbolic relation still holds. Separately, Herzog (1996) lists concrete limitations of
using force-length and force-velocity relationships to predict individual muscle force in
practice: the force-length relation is unknown for most human muscles, is plastic/adaptable
under elite training demands, differs between maximal and submaximal contraction, differs
with which length is held constant experimentally, and differs between electrically-stimulated
and voluntary contraction; the force-velocity relation is similarly unknown for individual
muscles, differs sharply between maximal and submaximal activation, differs between
force-controlled and velocity-controlled conditions, and inadequately accounts for
stretch-related (SSC) processes — stretch-shortening/plyometric force-velocity behavior
does not follow the standard inverse hyperbolic pattern at all (cf. Bosco 1982's finding
that plyometric training lets muscle produce more force after depth-jump training). Isometric
force itself also depends on contraction *history* (higher after a stretch than under pure
isometric hold, lower after a tension release), which is not captured in standard
force-velocity models. (PDF pp. 158-159, printed pp. 147-148, "3.3.2 The Effect of the Load
on Speed of Muscle Contraction," "Limitations of the Force-Velocity Relation," Fig 3.15.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism is offered for the Perrine-Edgerton deviation; the
text simply reports it as an empirical in vivo finding that conflicts with Hill's in vitro
model. **Inference:** possible contributors include the parallel elastic and series elastic
tissue contributions present in an intact human joint but not in isolated muscle
preparations, and the difficulty (noted by Herzog) of measuring true sarcomere-level length
and force in vivo, since sarcomeres do not behave linearly relative to whole muscle-tendon
length (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against treating the textbook hyperbolic
force-velocity curve as a precise predictive model for an individual athlete's real,
in vivo force output, especially near isometric/very-low-velocity conditions or for
stretch-shortening-cycle actions. It directly qualifies [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]]
(Ch1): the general specificity logic of that principle still holds, but the exact shape of
the curve near V=0 and under SSC conditions is more complex than the simple hyperbola implies.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry is marked **contested** deliberately: Hill's hyperbolic
model remains the standard, widely-taught simplification, and Perrine-Edgerton's in vivo
curve is one alternative dataset (1978), not a full replacement validated across muscle
groups and populations. Do not use this to discard force-velocity profiling broadly — it
is a caution about precision near the isometric end and under SSC conditions specifically,
not a rejection of the underlying force-velocity trade-off.

**Example** — A force-velocity profile built from isokinetic dynamometer data near zero
velocity should not be assumed to predict true 1RM isometric force accurately, per the
Perrine-Edgerton finding that peak torque actually occurs at a low, non-zero velocity
rather than at V=0.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
general principle this claim adds nuance and caveats to); [[claim--three-zone-force-velocity-curve-for-cyclic-locomotion]]
(a further, cyclic-specific deviation from Hill's model within this same Ch3 section).
