# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force — i.e.
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg — roughly two-thirds of their maximum**
— producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at true maximal
load, and time-to-complete-the-lift increased by 282% from the peak-power load to the
maximal load (Fig 3.17). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The Effect of the
Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no separate mechanism beyond noting the mismatch
between idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a

# In Cyclic Locomotion (Running/Walking), the Force-Velocity Curve Has Three Zones, Not One Hyperbola

**What it is** — Hill-type force-velocity work was mostly done on single-jointed exercises
or isolated muscle in vitro, excluding inertia and gravity effects on the whole limb and
body. The text notes poor transfer of speed-strength abilities from single-joint exercises
to natural multi-jointed movement under real gravity/inertia loading. Kuznetsov & Fiskalov
(1985) tested athletes running or walking on a treadmill at different speeds while pushing
against tensiometers, and found a force-velocity graph divisible into three zones (Fig
3.18), unlike Hill's single hyperbola: **Zone I**, similar to the classical inverse
hyperbolic relationship; **Zone II**, where force and velocity are approximately *directly*
proportional (force rises as velocity rises); and **Zone III**, where force and speed are
inversely related again, but not in Hill's hyperbolic form. The same study also found peak
force/torque is not necessarily produced under isometric conditions, agreeing with the
Perrine-Edgerton in vivo finding described separately. (PDF pp. 160, printed p. 149,
"Contraction Speed and Strength in Cyclic Activities," Fig 3.18.)

**Why it works** — No mechanism is given beyond attributing the deviation to the influence
of gravity and inertia acting on the whole limb/body system during cyclic locomotion,
conditions absent from isolated-muscle or single-joint isotonic testing; the practical
takeaway offered is that this shape lets researchers "select speed-strength exercises more
precisely for cyclic versus acyclic activities" and design training machines and force
production more accurately for each.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution against applying acyclic (single-joint,
isotonic-derived) force-velocity models to cyclic sport activities like sprinting,
swimming, or cycling; if profiling force-velocity characteristics for a cyclic-sport
athlete, expect a three-zone pattern rather than a single smooth hyperbola, particularly a
zone where force and velocity move together rather than trading off.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **contested** because this single 1985 study (Kuznetsov &
Fiskalov) directly conflicts with the classical Hill hyperbola that underlies
[[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1) and is itself a
different empirical deviation from the Perrine-Edgerton in vivo curve described in
[[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] — the book does not
reconcile all three pictures (Hill's hyperbola, Perrine-Edgerton's low-velocity peak, and
this three-zone cyclic curve) into one unified model, and none of the three should be
treated as the settled, final description of the human force-velocity relationship.

**Example** — A coach fitting a simple hyperbolic force-velocity profile to a sprinter's
treadmill-resisted-sprint data should not be surprised if the mid-velocity range shows
force and velocity rising together (Zone II) rather than trading off, per this cyclic-specific
finding.

classical model this contests); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(a separate, acyclic in vivo deviation from the same classical model, within this same Ch3
section).

# The Strength-Speed Continuum: Five Named Zones, and Why "Strength-Speed" ≠ "Speed-Strength"

**What it is** — Reading the force-velocity curve as a continuum from V=0 to very high V
identifies five distinct strength-related qualities: **isometric strength** (V=0),
**quasi-isometric strength** (very low velocity), **strength-speed** (low velocity),
**speed-strength** (intermediate velocity), and **explosive strength** (high velocity). The
text draws a deliberate, practically important distinction between the two middle terms,
which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The
Interrelation between Strength and Other Fitness Factors," Fig 3.21.)

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision — it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,
speed-emphasis power work, e.g. loaded jump squats at light load) rather than using
"speed-strength" as a catch-all. **Eric's baseline:** this refines the department's existing
Vermeil-hierarchy and general-to-specific programming language (`method-baseline.md`,
"Strength and power") by giving the strength-power continuum a finer, two-sided middle
category instead of one undifferentiated "power" zone between strength and speed.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a conceptual/terminological framework, not a validated
measurement scale — there is no stated velocity threshold separating "strength-speed" from
"speed-strength" in absolute units, so applying it requires judgment about where a given
exercise or athlete's task sits on the continuum rather than a hard cutoff. It also
explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which
sit outside the pure contractile force-velocity curve this continuum is built on.

**Example** — A heavy (70-80% 1RM) trapbar jump is strength-speed (strength-dominant power);
a loaded jump squat at 20-30% 1RM is speed-strength (speed-dominant power); both are
"explosive" in casual language, but this framework says they train different ends of the
same continuum and should not be programmed as interchangeable.

**Related** — [[principle--force-velocity-relationship-and-training-specificity]] (Ch1, the
underlying curve this continuum is read from); [[framework--types-of-maximal-strength]]
(Ch1, a different strength-ladder taxonomy — CFmax/TFmax/Fmm — not the same axis as this
velocity-based continuum); [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]]
(the stretch-reflex/tendon caveat that this continuum's underlying curves do not capture).

which are often used interchangeably: **strength-speed** describes training where speed
development matters but *strength* is the more important quality; **speed-strength**
describes training where speed development against resistance matters but *strength
acquisition* is comparatively less important. In physics terms, both correspond to power
(rate of doing work) and both distinguish these activities from longer-duration,
lower-intensity ones. Competitive categories mapped onto this continuum: cyclical
maximum-power short-duration events (sprinting, swimming, cycling); maximum-power sprint
activities with jumping/obstacles (hurdles); maximum-power activities against heavy loads
(weightlifting); maximum-power throwing activities (shotput, javelin); jumping activities;
and jumping activities with an implement (pole vault). The text also separately notes that
non-contractile elastic tissue (tendon) release and the myotatic stretch reflex are integral
to real speed-strength/strength-speed performance and are *not* captured by the Hill or
Perrine-Edgerton curves, which apply only to pure contractile-muscle force-velocity
behavior. (PDF pp. 161-163, printed pp. 150-152, "Speed-Strength and Strength-Speed," "The

**Why it works** — This is a terminology/classification framework rather than a
mechanistic claim; its value is definitional precision — it prevents conflating two
training emphases (speed-dominant vs. strength-dominant power development) that require
different exercise selection and loading even though both get colloquially called
"speed-strength."

**When to apply** — Use this distinction explicitly when writing programming language or
communicating with staff: label an exercise/block as targeting strength-speed (heavier,
strength-emphasis power work, e.g. heavy trap-bar jumps) versus speed-strength (lighter,

explicitly does not apply to stretch-reflex/tendon-elastic-energy-dominated actions, which

same continuum and should not be programmed as interchangeable.

# Small Changes in Joint Position Produce Large, Specific Changes in Force Output

**What it is** — A set of cited findings showing that limb/joint position, not just muscle
size or fitness, is a first-order determinant of measured or produced force: the pectineus
muscle's rotational action on the hip reverses direction depending on whether the hip is
flexing or extending (Baeyer, 1922); the sartorius can flex or extend the hip depending on
thigh position, and its correlation with hip flexor/extensor strength varies sharply by
angle (0.92 at 210° hip flexion vs. 0.41 at 90°; reverse pattern for extension, 0.86 at 90°
vs. 0.32 at 210°); forearm pronation reduces elbow-flexion strength by about one-third
(Rasch 1956; Wells 1960; Tricker 1967); and in the barbell clean from the ground, slight
elbow flexion reduces lifting force by 40%, a flexed trunk reduces it by 13.3%, and lateral
head tilt reduces it by an average of 9% (Sokolov, 1967). Separately, maximal knee-extension
force in a seated position occurs at a 160° knee angle (with force depending on hip angle),
but in a supine leg press, no difference in knee-extension force was found across a
100°-140° hip-angle range (Lindeburg, 1964); and knee-extension strength increases 10-12%
when the torso is inclined 20-25° backward from vertical in a seated rowing-style position
(Dorofeyev, 1965). (PDF pp. 163-164, printed pp. 152-153, "3.3.4 The Relationship between
Strength and Posture," "3.3.4.1 Strength Variation with Postural Change.")

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is leverage: joint angle changes the muscle's
operating length and the moment arm/leverage of the muscular force relative to the joint,
which changes the mechanical conditions of work — sometimes advantageously (full force
potential usable) and sometimes as a hindrance (only part of maximal tension usable).

**When to apply** — Use this as a quantified rationale for coaching cues that treat small
positional details (elbow lockout during the pull, trunk angle, head/neck position) as
directly consequential for force output and bar path in Olympic-lift-family and clean-pattern
movements, not merely aesthetic technique points. **Eric's baseline:** relevant to any
coaching of the clean/pull pattern in Baylor's strength programming and to interpreting
joint-angle-specific force-plate or isokinetic data (e.g. why a knee-extension test result
at one angle should not be assumed to predict force at another angle or in a different
exercise, per the Lindeburg finding above).

**When NOT to apply** — These are old, mostly single-study citations (1922-1967) on
specific joints and populations; the precise percentages (40%, 13.3%, 9%, 10-12%) should
be treated as illustrative of the *existence and rough size* of position effects, not as
precise, universally-applicable corrections. Angle-strength relationships are also
exercise-specific (the same knee joint behaves differently in a seated versus supine task
per Lindeburg), so findings from one exercise should not be transferred to another without
verification.

**Example** — A 9% strength reduction from lateral head tilt alone (Sokolov, 1967) is a
concrete, citable reason to coach a neutral head position during a maximal clean attempt,
beyond generic "keep your head neutral" cueing.

**Related** — [[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]] (Ch1, the general
torque/leverage principle this claim supplies specific joint-angle examples for);
[[principle--pelvic-tilt-is-task-specific-not-universal]] (the pelvis-specific continuation
of this same posture discussion, 3.3.4.2).

# There Is No Single "Correct" Pelvic Tilt: The Right Tilt Depends on the Movement Phase

**What it is** — The pelvis is the key link between spine and lower extremities, and
inappropriate orientation can create an unstable or weak base and expose the lumbar discs
to injury, particularly under spinal flexion or flexion-plus-rotation. The text directly
challenges the common fitness-industry instruction that a single "correct" (usually
posterior) pelvic tilt applies to all movement: there is a **lumbar-pelvic rhythm** in
which the appropriate tilt changes synchronously through a lift (Cailliet, 1981), confirmed
by video, force-plate, and EMG analysis of weightlifters and powerlifters. Using the
"iliac crest" convention: **posterior pelvic tilt** is appropriate for sit-ups or lifting
objects from above waist level; **anterior pelvic tilt** is the correct rotation for
squatting, lifting heavy loads off the floor, or toe-touching — and starting a lift or
squat with a *posterior* tilt is specifically flagged as dangerous, since it causes lumbar
flexion and exposes the discs. The pelvis actually rotates in three dimensions (X-axis =
anterior-posterior tilt; Z-axis = side-to-side iliac-crest rocking, natural in walking but
risky if it occurs during squatting, overhead pressing, or deadlifting; Y-axis = rotation
that occurs naturally in walking, running, throwing, and kicking, but is harmful to the
lumbar spine under high load or momentum, especially combined with rotation on other axes).
"Neutral" pelvic tilt is explicitly reframed as a *reference standard* for static
standing/sitting/walking, not automatically "the safest position for all movement." (PDF
pp. 164-166, printed pp. 153-155, "3.3.4.2 Strength, Safety and Pelvic Tilt," Fig 3.22.)

**Why it works** — Maintaining the lumbar spine's neutral curvature (not necessarily a
neutral *pelvis*) under load is the actual safety goal; because the pelvis's relationship
to the spine changes with body position (standing vs. leaning vs. supine vs. prone) and
task demand (lifting vs. sitting vs. rotating), a single fixed pelvic position cannot
preserve neutral lumbar curvature across all of those tasks — hence the tilt itself has to
change with the phase and type of movement to keep the actual protective goal (safe lumbar
curvature) constant.

**When to apply** — Use this to correct blanket "posterior pelvic tilt" or "brace neutral"
coaching cues applied identically to sit-ups and to floor-based lifts (deadlift, clean
pull, squat): the text's own biomechanical analysis argues these need opposite tilt cues.
**Eric's baseline:** directly relevant to Baylor's barbell coaching (clean, snatch, squat,
deadlift patterns referenced throughout the S&C curriculum material) and to any staff
in-service on lifting technique cues, since this gives a specific, citable rationale for
differentiating tilt cues by lift and by phase rather than using one universal cue.

**When NOT to apply** — This is Siff's own synthesis built primarily on one cited source
(Cailliet, 1981) plus general biomechanical reasoning, not a randomized or outcome-controlled
study of injury rates under different tilt cues; treat the specific "posterior tilt for
sit-ups, anterior tilt for squats/deadlifts" rule as a reasoned coaching heuristic backed
by video/EMG description, not as a proven injury-prevention intervention with measured
outcomes. It also does not address every possible lifting pattern (e.g. Olympic pulling
positions), where the same reasoning would need to be worked through separately.

**Example** — Cueing a lifter to "tuck the pelvis under" (posterior tilt) at the start of a
deadlift or squat, following generic core-bracing advice borrowed from ab-training cues,
is exactly the error this section warns against — the text argues that specific setup
should use an anterior tilt at the iliac crest instead.

**Related** — [[claim--joint-angle-and-limb-position-changes-force-output]] (the preceding
subsection's general posture-and-force-output findings); [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]]
(the next subsection's continuation of the same postural-safety discussion).

# Coach Head and Eye Position Deliberately During Barbell Lifts — It Drives Spinal Reflexes and Balance

**What it is** — Head position has a powerful, largely reflexive effect on posture and
lifting safety. Flexing the neck causes a **reflex relaxation of the back's erector
muscles**, which is dangerous during resisted lifts (squatting, cleaning, deadlifting), so
a deliberate degree of neck extension is needed to facilitate strong erector contraction
during ground-based pulls — but not so much as to hyperextend/hollow the back, which
loads the spinal discs asymmetrically. During skilled Olympic-lift phases, specific head
errors have specific consequences: throwing the head back prematurely during the pull can
pull the bar too far from the body; tilting the head back during the jerk can cause the
lift to be lost forward; tilting the head back to look up at the bar during the snatch's
low-squat fixation can cause the lifter to fall backward and lose the lift; and dropping
the head down during the squat can push the lumbar spine into a hyperflexed, injury-risk

# Some Movement Asymmetry Is Natural and Safe; Chasing Perfect Bilateral Symmetry Can Backfire

**What it is** — Because of genuine structural and functional body asymmetry, a single
"correct," perfectly symmetric technique enforced on every athlete "may seriously diminish
an athlete's performance." In lifting, the bar routinely rotates or tilts slightly to one
side rather than traveling perfectly parallel to the frontal/sagittal/transverse planes,
and this is described as natural rather than a flaw to eliminate — coaches should learn to
distinguish natural, harmless asymmetry from genuinely inefficient or unsafe deviation, in
part by observing and recording bar trajectory from both sides of the body and comparing it
to the ideal trajectory, rather than assuming any visible asymmetry is a problem. The text
explicitly cautions that **relying on isokinetic or similar devices to measure
agonist/antagonist or left/right strength ratios in order to "correct" so-called imbalances
"may be unproductive and ill-advised."** (PDF p. 166, printed pp. 155-156, "3.3.4.4
Strength, Symmetry and Limb Alignment"; symmetric training itself is deferred to Ch4.2.8.)

**Why it works** — No formal mechanism is given beyond the general point that
individualized body structure, muscle composition, and neuromuscular control make a
uniform symmetric ideal biomechanically unrealistic for many athletes, and that isokinetic
symmetry testing measures an isolated, single-joint proxy that may not represent
functional, whole-movement asymmetry accurately or usefully.

**When to apply** — Use this as a caution before flagging or "correcting" an athlete's
L/R asymmetry purely because a test shows a numeric difference: first establish, via
technique observation (e.g. bar-path video from both sides), whether the asymmetry is a
natural individual pattern or an actual inefficiency/injury-risk deviation.

**When NOT to apply — direct tension with current Baylor practice.** This claim sits in
real tension with the department's own testing framework: the HD ODSF metric-selection
model explicitly includes symmetry (L/R differences) as an optional force-plate reporting
category (`method-baseline.md`, "Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring," citing
`hd-odsf-metrics.md`), and force-plate/isokinetic symmetry indices are in active use for
rehab and return-to-play decisions. **Eric's review would be needed** to reconcile this
1990s-2009-era caution against isokinetic-symmetry-based "correction" with the department's
modern use of symmetry metrics; this entry does not resolve that tension, it only flags it
— the book's objection is specifically to *using an isokinetic ratio to drive a
correction*, which is a narrower target than symmetry monitoring for RTP tracking purposes
more broadly, but Eric's own view on where that line falls is not stated anywhere in the
corpus reviewed for `method-baseline.md`.

**Example** — A force-plate report showing a 12% L/R asymmetry in a healthy, high-performing
athlete with no injury history or technique flaw, per this claim, is not automatically
something to "fix" — the text would ask whether that asymmetry reflects a natural,
individual movement pattern before prescribing corrective unilateral work.

**Related** — [[heuristic--head-and-eye-position-cues-for-barbell-lifts]] (the preceding
subsection, same overall posture-and-technique section); Ch4.2.8 "The Concept of Symmetric
Training" (explicitly deferred by the text itself — not yet ingested, future chapter).

category: [strength, testing, anthropometrics]

# Allometric Scaling Laws Let You Compare Strength Fairly Across Bodymass (and Height) Classes

**What it is** — Because bodymass scales with the cube of linear body dimensions while
muscle cross-sectional area (and thus force capacity) scales only with the square, maximum
strength (F) and bodymass (B) are theoretically related by F = a.B^(2/3) (Lietzke, 1956,
found a best-fit exponent of 0.6748, close to the theoretical 0.6667). Historical
weight-class-comparison formulas built on this (Hoffman's two-thirds-power formula, the
Austin 3/4-exponent formula, McSorley's and Sinclair's parabolic tables) each had accuracy
limits, especially extrapolating to heavier lifters. Siff (1988) fit sigmoid/power-law
curves to the mean of the ten best all-time lifts per bodymass class (up to ~165 kg) and
found a power-law equation, **Total T = a - b.B^(-c)**, fit weightlifting and powerlifting
records with R > 0.996 in all cases (distinct constants given for weightlifting total,
powerlifting total, squat, bench, and deadlift); separate equations were fit for juvenile
lifters (logistic form) and for women (exponential form). Using these equations, an
athlete's Total can be expressed as a percentage of the world-class total for their exact
bodymass, enabling fair cross-weight-class comparison and longitudinal tracking even as an
athlete's bodymass itself changes. Analysis of the equations shows **relative strength
(strength per unit bodymass) actually peaks at a bodymass of 60-67 kg** in elite
weightlifters/powerlifters, not at either extreme. A related but weaker relationship: for a
given bodymass, taller lifters tend to be *less* strong at elite level (an exponential
height-bodymass equation is given per build class, Table 3.5); and the bodymass-strength
correlation weakens as movement speed increases (0.719 for the slow press vs. 0.706 clean-and-jerk
vs. 0.685 snatch), meaning bodymass predicts maximal-strength lifts much better than
fast, technical ones. (PDF pp. 166-171, printed pp. 155-160, "3.3.5 The Dependence of
Strength on Bodymass," "3.3.6 The Relationship between Strength and Height," Tables 3.3-3.5,
Figs 3.23-3.24.)

**Why it works** — The scaling logic is dimensional analysis, not an empirical fit per se:
strength derives from muscle cross-sectional area (a squared, two-dimensional quantity)
while bodymass derives from volume (a cubed, three-dimensional quantity) for
geometrically-similar bodies, so absolute strength cannot keep pace linearly with bodymass
as size increases — larger athletes are stronger in absolute terms but structurally
disadvantaged in relative-strength terms past a certain point, which is also the
underlying reason taller athletes at a fixed bodymass (thinner build for their height) tend
to be relatively weaker.

**When to apply** — Use the underlying two-thirds-power scaling logic (well-established,
independent of this text, in exercise-science literature on cross-weight-class
comparison) whenever normalizing strength testing data across athletes of different
bodymass — e.g. comparing back-squat 1RM across a football roster spanning 180-320+ lb
linemen to skill players is misleading without some bodymass adjustment, and simple
per-kg relative strength (load/bodymass) is itself an approximation that over- or
under-corrects depending where an athlete sits on this curve. **Eric's baseline:** relevant
to the department's stated need for sport-specific, threshold-contextualized data (currently
a named gap per `performance-playbook-development-plan.md` 3.2.3) — a bodymass-adjusted
strength-comparison method, even a simplified version of Siff's approach, would be a
concrete way to build fairer cross-position strength benchmarks for football specifically.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific numeric constants (a, b, c values) are fit to
weightlifting and powerlifting records through 1987-1988 and to Russian weightlifter height
data of that era — they should not be applied directly to football or other sport
populations without refitting to relevant data; the underlying two-thirds power law
scaling principle is well-established and broadly applicable, but the exact equations and
the "60-67 kg relative-strength peak" finding are specific to Olympic/power lifters of
that period and should be treated as illustrative, not directly transferable.

**Example** — Comparing a 90 kg lifter's 405 kg powerlifting total to a 140 kg lifter's 500
kg total by raw numbers alone favors the heavier lifter; converting each to a percentage of
the world-class total expected at their own bodymass (via Table 3.3's fitted curve) gives a
fairer relative-strength comparison, which is the entire point of this scaling approach.

**Related** — [[claim--strength-age-relationship-and-adjustment-equations]] (the next
subsection's parallel age-adjustment method, explicitly combined with this bodymass
adjustment in the book's own worked example); [[claim--female-male-strength-ratio-varies-by-muscle-group-and-bodymass]]
(uses the same bodymass-normalization logic for sex comparison).

versus dynamometer testing of one isolated muscle group (usually quadriceps). Linear
regression fits the 30-80 age decline for each dataset: for untrained lab subjects, %S =
120.17 - 0.68865A (R=0.988); for trained weightlifters, %S = 140.15 - 1.3853A (R=0.996),

decline per year for those who had reached a higher peak, even though both groups decline
by roughly the same fraction. A worked example combines this with the bodymass-adjustment
equations (3.3.5) to show a 45-year-old, 80 kg lifter with a 260 kg total (87.1%
age-and-bodymass-adjusted score) can have *greater* relative strength than a young 90 kg
lifter with a 350 kg total (86.3% bodymass-adjusted, no age adjustment needed) — illustrating

testing vs. whole-body competitive lifting) mean the two methods are not measuring
identical constructs, especially where technical skill and multi-joint coordination (more

still-developing young lifters) partially compensates for or masks the underlying raw

# Allometric Scaling Laws Let You Compare Strength Fairly Across Bodymass (and Height) Classes

**What it is** — Because bodymass scales with the cube of linear body dimensions while
muscle cross-sectional area (and thus force capacity) scales only with the square, maximum

# Female Strength Is ~2/3 of Male at Equal Bodymass on Average, but the Ratio Is Not Uniform

**What it is** — Women's strength averages roughly two-thirds that of men at the same
bodymass and age, both sexes peaking at about the same age; this is attributed mainly to
males' greater percentage of lean muscle mass, since strength *per unit muscle
cross-sectional area* is essentially equal between sexes (cited as ~4 kg per sq cm for
both). But the ratio is not constant: comparing top-five all-time weightlifting totals by
bodymass class, the female/male ratio **decreases as bodymass increases** — 0.76 at 52 kg,
0.72 at 56 kg, 0.70 at 60 kg, 0.67 at 67.5 kg, 0.64 at 75 kg, 0.63 at 82.5 kg, down to 0.59
at 104.9 kg (Table 3.7) — meaning added bodymass produces disproportionately more strength
gain in men than in women. The ratio also varies sharply by muscle group (Hettinger, 1961,
Table 3.8): elbow flexors/extensors 0.55 (women weakest relative to men here), trunk
flexors/extensors 0.60, finger flexors/ankle extensors 0.60, finger adductors/knee
extensors 0.65, deltoids/hand flexors-extensors 0.75, knee flexors/masticating muscles
0.60, and hip flexors/extensors 0.80 (the smallest sex gap of any group tested). The text
notes these ratios likely partly reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between
average men and women of that era, and that such differences are expected to shrink or
disappear among similarly-trained male and female athletes. (PDF p. 172, printed pp.
161-162, "3.3.8 The Relationship between Strength and Gender," Tables 3.7-3.8.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is compositional, not contractile: equal
force-per-cross-sectional-area between sexes means the sex strength gap is driven almost
entirely by *how much* muscle each sex typically carries (lean mass percentage), not by any
difference in muscle tissue quality — which is also why the gap shrinks in upper-body/arm
musculature least (where habitual-use and lean-mass differences are largest, per the text's
own caveat) and shrinks most in hip flexors/extensors (where daily-life use is more similar
between sexes).

**When to apply** — Use the muscle-group-specific ratio table, not a single blanket "2/3"
figure, when setting relative starting loads or interpreting strength-test disparities by
exercise/muscle group for female athletes — the text itself frames Table 3.8 as a guide for
"selecting suitable starting loads for female trainees." **Eric's baseline:** relevant
context for the department's existing choice to default women's-sport strength testing to
repetition-max rather than 1RM protocols (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"
citing week1-lecture.md p.39) — this table gives a physiological rationale for why a single
sex-adjustment ratio would be inaccurate across different lifts/muscle groups if the
department ever wanted to build sex-specific relative-strength benchmarks by exercise.

**When NOT to apply** — These ratios come from historical (pre-1988) competition records
and a single 1961 lab study (Hettinger), collected before the substantial expansion of
women's competitive strength sports; the text's own caveat that trained-athlete gaps likely
differ from these general-population/historical-competitor gaps should be taken seriously —
these numbers should not be used as fixed sex-adjustment constants for a modern, well-trained
athlete population without re-verification.

**Example** — Using a flat "give women 67% of the men's load" rule for every exercise would
overload the elbow flexors/extensors relative to the actual sex gap there (0.55) and
underload the hip flexors/extensors relative to their actual, much smaller gap (0.80), per
Table 3.8.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the bodymass-normalization
method this sex comparison is layered on top of).

# Elite Lifting Performance Rose Steadily by Decade (Gompertz Curve); the Press's Faster Growth May Reflect Steroid Use

**What it is** — Normalizing weightlifting performance across all bodymass divisions (as a
percentage of the mean of the ten heaviest totals ever recorded per division, via the
bodymass-scaling equation from 3.3.5) and plotting the result by year from 1950-1990 shows a
**Gompertz growth curve** (Points y = a.e^(-b.e^(-cx)), x = year-1950) fits the historical
rise in performance well for the snatch, clean-and-jerk, and press (R = 0.994-0.996 for
each, with separate fitted constants a, b, c per lift). The snatch and clean-and-jerk show a
similar growth trend, but the **press grew measurably faster**. Since the Olympic press was
removed from competition in 1971, its longer-term trend cannot be studied further. (PDF pp.
172-173, printed pp. 161-162, "3.3.9 The Increase in Human Strength over Time," Fig 3.26.)

**Why it works** — The Gompertz form itself is a standard actuarial/biological growth-curve
choice for processes with an early accelerating phase followed by a plateau approaching some
ceiling — it fits generic athletic-record progression patterns generally, not something
specific to strength physiology. For the *differential* growth rate between lifts, the text
offers an explicitly labeled interpretation, not a proven mechanism: Siff and Medvedev
"have both suggested that the discrepancy possibly lies in the widespread use of anabolic
substances since the late 1950s," reasoning that the press is slower, more
quasi-isometric, and more dependent on muscle hypertrophy and relative strength than the
more technically-demanding snatch and clean-and-jerk, and that anabolic substances would be
expected to preferentially benefit hypertrophy-dependent, technically-simpler lifts (also
naming the powerlifting squat, bench press, and deadlift as lifts that would be expected to
benefit similarly).

**When to apply** — The Gompertz-curve secular-trend finding itself is useful background for
understanding why raw historical strength-record comparisons across decades are misleading
without normalizing for era; the steroid explanation should be treated and cited
specifically as the authors' own **speculative interpretation** of a correlational pattern
(different growth rates for different lifts), not as an established causal finding.

**When NOT to apply** — The steroid-use explanation is explicitly hedged by the authors
themselves ("it is reasonable to expect...") and is not a tested causal claim — no doping
prevalence data, testing records, or controlled comparison is presented to support it
directly; it should be reported as the authors' own inference from an indirect pattern
(differential growth rates by lift type), never as a confirmed finding. The Gompertz fit
itself is also a single dataset ending in 1990 and should not be extrapolated to predict
current-era performance ceilings without updated data.

**Example** — Citing "weightlifting has improved steadily since 1950 per a Gompertz growth
model" is a supportable, quantified historical claim; citing "the press grew faster because
of steroids" as an established fact (rather than "Siff and Medvedev's own hypothesis, based
on the press's lower technical demand") would overstate what this section actually shows.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the same normalization method
used to build this secular-trend dataset).

# Female Strength Is ~2/3 of Male at Equal Bodymass on Average, but the Ratio Is Not Uniform

**What it is** — Women's strength averages roughly two-thirds that of men at the same
bodymass and age, both sexes peaking at about the same age; this is attributed mainly to
males' greater percentage of lean muscle mass, since strength *per unit muscle
cross-sectional area* is essentially equal between sexes (cited as ~4 kg per sq cm for
both). But the ratio is not constant: comparing top-five all-time weightlifting totals by
bodymass class, the female/male ratio **decreases as bodymass increases** — 0.76 at 52 kg,
0.72 at 56 kg, 0.70 at 60 kg, 0.67 at 67.5 kg, 0.64 at 75 kg, 0.63 at 82.5 kg, down to 0.59
at 104.9 kg (Table 3.7) — meaning added bodymass produces disproportionately more strength
gain in men than in women. The ratio also varies sharply by muscle group (Hettinger, 1961,
Table 3.8): elbow flexors/extensors 0.55 (women weakest relative to men here), trunk
flexors/extensors 0.60, finger flexors/ankle extensors 0.60, finger adductors/knee
extensors 0.65, deltoids/hand flexors-extensors 0.75, knee flexors/masticating muscles
0.60, and hip flexors/extensors 0.80 (the smallest sex gap of any group tested). The text
notes these ratios likely partly reflect differing habitual daily-life activity between
average men and women of that era, and that such differences are expected to shrink or
disappear among similarly-trained male and female athletes. (PDF p. 172, printed pp.
161-162, "3.3.8 The Relationship between Strength and Gender," Tables 3.7-3.8.)

**Why it works** — The stated mechanism is compositional, not contractile: equal
force-per-cross-sectional-area between sexes means the sex strength gap is driven almost
entirely by *how much* muscle each sex typically carries (lean mass percentage), not by any
difference in muscle tissue quality — which is also why the gap shrinks in upper-body/arm
musculature least (where habitual-use and lean-mass differences are largest, per the text's
own caveat) and shrinks most in hip flexors/extensors (where daily-life use is more similar
between sexes).

**When to apply** — Use the muscle-group-specific ratio table, not a single blanket "2/3"
figure, when setting relative starting loads or interpreting strength-test disparities by
exercise/muscle group for female athletes — the text itself frames Table 3.8 as a guide for
"selecting suitable starting loads for female trainees." **Eric's baseline:** relevant
context for the department's existing choice to default women's-sport strength testing to
repetition-max rather than 1RM protocols (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment,"
citing week1-lecture.md p.39) — this table gives a physiological rationale for why a single
sex-adjustment ratio would be inaccurate across different lifts/muscle groups if the
department ever wanted to build sex-specific relative-strength benchmarks by exercise.

**When NOT to apply** — These ratios come from historical (pre-1988) competition records
and a single 1961 lab study (Hettinger), collected before the substantial expansion of
women's competitive strength sports; the text's own caveat that trained-athlete gaps likely
differ from these general-population/historical-competitor gaps should be taken seriously —
these numbers should not be used as fixed sex-adjustment constants for a modern, well-trained
athlete population without re-verification.

**Example** — Using a flat "give women 67% of the men's load" rule for every exercise would
overload the elbow flexors/extensors relative to the actual sex gap there (0.55) and
underload the hip flexors/extensors relative to their actual, much smaller gap (0.80), per
Table 3.8.

**Related** — [[framework--bodymass-strength-scaling-laws]] (the bodymass-normalization
method this sex comparison is layered on top of).

# Warm-Up Works Through Temperature and CNS Priming, and Its Value Is Event- and Training-Status-Specific

**What it is** — The warm-up has two components: **general** (raising the body's overall
functional potential) and **specific** (establishing the optimal relationship between the
CNS and the upcoming movement). The text argues "warm-up" is a misleading name, since the
CNS-priming role can matter more than literal tissue warming, and proposes "pre-activity
preparation" as a more accurate term, covering neural priming, physical tissue warming, and
psychological readying. **Temperature mechanism**: muscle contracts faster and more
intensely as temperature rises within a safe range, and electrical muscle activity rises
with body temperature (Golenhofen & Goptert 1958; Book & Golenhofen 1959); a hot shower
increases isometric endurance and cyclic-work speed/endurance by 7.5-9.0%; cooling to 18°C
shortens muscular work capacity 2-3x; massage does not change cyclic endurance but does
increase explosive-work power. **Activity-specific evidence**: active, intense warm-ups
(not moderate-intensity ones) effectively prepare for speed-strength/explosive work,
producing measured gains such as +1.0-4.5 cm in women's basketball jumps, up to +10 cm in
long jump, +400-700 N boxing punch force with 0.02-0.04 s faster striking time, and
correlation between rest interval and punch force rising from R=0.40 (no warm-up) to
R=0.62 (after warm-up). Franks' literature summary (cited via Williams, 1983) gives the
governing decision rules: high-intensity short-duration events (weightlifting, shotput)
benefit from warming up; vigorous warm-up can *hurt* endurance-sport performance; low-intensity/endurance
athletes gain little from warming up; direct warm-ups (task-similar activity) at moderate
intensity/duration help trained athletes in explosive sports but not necessarily untrained
ones; indirect warm-ups (unrelated activity, e.g. cycling, stretching) can help if kept
unstressful; nearly all studies showing warm-up as *detrimental* used untrained subjects
who could not tolerate high-intensity warm-ups; and strenuous, non-specific warm-ups can
interfere with motor-skill-dependent sports. (PDF pp. 173-176, printed pp. 162-165,
"3.4 Factors Increasing the Working Effect of Strength," "3.4.1 The Warm-up and
Pre-Activity Preparation.")

**Why it works** — Temperature effects act at the muscle-fibre level (contraction speed and
force rise with safe-range temperature increases, and post-stimulation active-state
duration shortens with heat); the CNS-priming component works by establishing task-specific
neural readiness before the main effort, which is why "little or no general physical
warming up may be necessary" for sports (Olympic lifting, gymnastics) whose competitive
movements themselves double as adequate specific preparation, and why endurance events
(marathon) need essentially no dedicated specific warm-up since the event itself provides it.

**When to apply** — Use the Franks decision rules directly when designing warm-up protocols
by sport/session type: prescribe active, direct (task-similar), moderate-to-high-intensity
warm-ups before explosive/power/max-strength work for trained athletes specifically, and
favor lighter, indirect warm-ups (or none) before pure endurance work. **Eric's baseline:**
directly usable to formalize warm-up prescription language in Baylor's own S&C
programming and in the HHPR 5355 curriculum material, since the department's documented
practice does not currently specify a warm-up decision framework distinct from general
programming guidance.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific performance-gain numbers (jump height, punch force,
strike time) are single old studies on specific populations (women's basketball, boxers,
long jumpers) and should be treated as illustrative magnitude, not as guaranteed or
individually-applicable gains. The Franks rules are themselves a literature summary from
1983 sources, not a fresh meta-analysis; they capture broad, still-plausible patterns but
should be applied as heuristics, not fixed thresholds.

**Example** — Prescribing a long, generalized, non-specific dynamic warm-up before a
football lineman's max-effort squat testing session risks the "strenuous, non-specific
warm-up interferes with skill" failure mode per Franks; a shorter, direct (squat-pattern-specific)
warm-up ramping intensity toward the working weight better fits this framework's guidance
for trained athletes in an explosive/max-strength task.

**Related** — [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the
immediately following subsection, on how a *specific prior strength stimulus* — not just a
general warm-up — further boosts subsequent performance).

# Post-Tetanic (Post-Activation) Potentiation: Optimal Load, Timing Window, and Sequencing Rules

**What it is** — When a muscle is stimulated by a series of impulses, its subsequent
activity is measurably altered — a phenomenon called (in Western physiology) post-tetanic
potentiation, produced by a preceding maximal/near-tetanic stimulus. The Russian-literature
findings the text emphasizes: **sequencing matters** — preliminary isometric tension
followed by dynamic work improves the dynamic work (up to 20% effectiveness increase
despite fatigue), but the *reverse* sequence (dynamic then isometric) does not show the
same improvement; the effect appears from the very first subsequent contraction (with a
residual inhibitory trace on the first rep) and strengthens sharply by the second
contraction. **Optimal load** (moderately-qualified athletes): the largest post-isometric
dynamic-strength boost (90%) came after a 50% 1RM stimulus; 25% 1RM produced only a 6.7%
boost and 100% 1RM only 5.8% — "the optimal and not the maximal load is necessary for
obtaining the greatest post-work improvement" — though with rising fitness, larger loads
(up to 100% max) can start producing the post-work improvement too (Ilin, 1961). **Timing
window** depends on the conditioning stimulus: after tonic barbell-squat work, explosive
isometric force rose 25% within the first minute and continued rising to 65% after 4-5
minutes (time-to-peak-force also dropped 2.6% immediately, 4.6% after 3-4 minutes); for
vertical jump specifically, barbell squats potentiated jump height by 6.8% at 3-4 minutes
post, while depth jumps potentiated jump height by 8.0% but peaked later, at 8-10 minutes
post. Higher-load isometric stimuli (100% 1RM) took *longest* to reach peak potentiation
(15.4 min) versus 50% 1RM (17.2 min, longest) versus 25% 1RM (12 min, fastest) in one
dataset (Ilin, 1961) — so the load-to-timing relationship is not perfectly monotonic
across every study cited. **Rest interval**: optimal weightlifting inter-set rest during
the after-effect window is 2-5 minutes, increasing with the lifter's bodymass; weightlifters
who carefully time rest intervals make 20% fewer failed lifts than those who do not
(Klimonov, 1965). **Delayed effects**: moderate-volume barbell work produces a positive
tonic effect the next day or two; depth (plyometric) jumps delay their facilitative effect
by 5-6 days. (PDF pp. 175-178, printed pp. 164-166, "3.4.2 The After-Effect of Muscle
Activity," Figs 3.27-3.29.)

**Why it works** — The text frames this as a nervous-system "after-effect" or "trace"
phenomenon: any stimulus, momentary or not, leaves a lingering trace in the nervous system
reflecting its relative inertness, which is proposed as foundational to how fitness
continues rising despite periodic breaks in training; the isometric-then-dynamic sequencing
effect is attributed to this same central trace mechanism rather than to a purely local
muscular effect, since the effect shows up in the CNS's general "toning" influence on the
motor apparatus, not just the specific muscle stimulated.

**When to apply** — Use this as a concrete, quantified starting template for complex/contrast
training design (heavy strength stimulus paired with an explosive movement): favor ~50% 1RM
isometric or heavy-tonic conditioning stimuli over maximal loads for athletes not yet highly
trained; expect the potentiation window to open within 1 minute and build over several
minutes, with the peak timing shifting later (toward 8-10 minutes) for a more demanding
stimulus like depth jumps versus barbell squats; and program the explosive/dynamic movement
*after* the conditioning stimulus, never the reverse order, per the sequencing finding.
**Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this offers a citable, historically-grounded
starting point (a squat-then-jump contrast pair with a 3-5 minute rest window) if the
department wants to formalize a PAP/complex-training protocol, to be validated against the
department's own force-plate (CMJ) data on actual athletes before being adopted as policy.

**When NOT to apply** — All quantified figures here come from single, older Russian studies
(Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961; Klimonov 1965) on specific lifts (barbell squat, isometric leg
extension) and specific populations; the load-to-timing relationship is shown as
non-monotonic in at least one dataset (25% 1RM peaking fastest, 50% slowest), so this
should not be flattened into a single simple "heavier load = later peak" rule. This
framework should be read alongside [[claim--pap-findings-contested-western-vs-russian-literature]],
which documents that Western studies of the same general phenomenon found much weaker or
absent effects — the sequencing/timing rules here reflect the Russian dataset specifically,
not a universally-replicated finding.

later by depth jumps (or vice versa, testing depth-jump-first conditioning with an 8-10

# Whether a Prior Heavy Stimulus Reliably Boosts Subsequent Performance Is Genuinely Contested Across the Cited Literature

**What it is** — The text explicitly flags that "research into the after-effects of
muscular activity is contradictory, particularly in Western literature." Cited findings on
both sides, within the same short passage: a statistically significant increase in
unloaded-movement speed directly after the same movement performed with added weight
(Murray, 1959; Van Huss et al, 1962) — but other research found **no such effect**, despite
subjective athlete reports that movements "felt quicker" after using loads (Nofsinger,
1963; Nelson & Lambert, 1965); no measurable increase in vertical jump shortly after
preceding resistive exercise (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965); and shot-put results that actually
**deteriorated** after preliminary throws with a heavier shot (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).
By contrast, the Russian-literature studies detailed in
[[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (Tatian 1964; Ilin 1961;
Diachkov 1961 and others) consistently report positive potentiation effects with specific
load, timing, and sequencing parameters. The text does not reconcile these two literatures
or explain the discrepancy. (PDF p. 176, printed p. 164-165, "3.4.2 The After-Effect of
Muscle Activity.")

**Why it works** — No mechanism for the disagreement is offered by the author.
**Inference:** plausible contributors (not stated in the text) could include differences in
the specific loads, rest intervals, and movements tested across studies, differences in
subject training status, or measurement sensitivity — but since the book itself does not
investigate or resolve this, any explanation beyond "the cited Western and Russian studies
disagree" would be unsupported speculation.

**When to apply** — Cite this contested status explicitly whenever presenting
post-activation-potentiation research to Baylor staff: the specific, quantified
prescriptions in [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] come
from the Russian side of a literature that, by this book's own account, does not uniformly
agree the phenomenon shows up as measured, even for broadly similar movements (jumps,
throws). This matters directly for how confidently a PAP/complex-training protocol should
be presented to coaches as "evidence-based."

**When NOT to apply** — Do not treat this contested framing as evidence that PAP "doesn't
work" — the disagreement runs in the specific direction of some Western studies finding no
effect or a negative effect under their own testing conditions, not a general finding that
potentiation never occurs; nor should it be read as proof the Russian findings are simply
correct and the Western ones flawed. The most honest reading, per the brief's rule against
harmonizing conflicting sources, is that the *net direction and reliability* of PAP under
any specific protocol needs verification with the department's own athletes and equipment
before being trusted as a general effect.

**Example** — If a Baylor coach cites "post-activation potentiation reliably boosts vertical
jump" as settled science, this entry is the citable correction: even within this one book's
own review of the (dated) literature, at least one cited study found no jump-height increase
at all after a resistive-exercise stimulus (Stockholm & Nelson, 1965), and another found a
throwing event's performance got worse (Bischke & Morehouse, 1950).

**Related** — [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the
Russian-literature-based prescription this claim directly qualifies).

# Warm-Up Works Through Temperature and CNS Priming, and Its Value Is Event- and Training-Status-Specific

**What it is** — The warm-up has two components: **general** (raising the body's overall
functional potential) and **specific** (establishing the optimal relationship between the
CNS and the upcoming movement). The text argues "warm-up" is a misleading name, since the
CNS-priming role can matter more than literal tissue warming, and proposes "pre-activity
preparation" as a more accurate term, covering neural priming, physical tissue warming, and
psychological readying. **Temperature mechanism**: muscle contracts faster and more
intensely as temperature rises within a safe range, and electrical muscle activity rises
with body temperature (Golenhofen & Goptert 1958; Book & Golenhofen 1959); a hot shower
increases isometric endurance and cyclic-work speed/endurance by 7.5-9.0%; cooling to 18°C
shortens muscular work capacity 2-3x; massage does not change cyclic endurance but does
increase explosive-work power. **Activity-specific evidence**: active, intense warm-ups
(not moderate-intensity ones) effectively prepare for speed-strength/explosive work,
producing measured gains such as +1.0-4.5 cm in women's basketball jumps, up to +10 cm in
long jump, +400-700 N boxing punch force with 0.02-0.04 s faster striking time, and
correlation between rest interval and punch force rising from R=0.40 (no warm-up) to
R=0.62 (after warm-up). Franks' literature summary (cited via Williams, 1983) gives the
governing decision rules: high-intensity short-duration events (weightlifting, shotput)
benefit from warming up; vigorous warm-up can *hurt* endurance-sport performance; low-intensity/endurance
athletes gain little from warming up; direct warm-ups (task-similar activity) at moderate
intensity/duration help trained athletes in explosive sports but not necessarily untrained
ones; indirect warm-ups (unrelated activity, e.g. cycling, stretching) can help if kept
unstressful; nearly all studies showing warm-up as *detrimental* used untrained subjects
who could not tolerate high-intensity warm-ups; and strenuous, non-specific warm-ups can
interfere with motor-skill-dependent sports. (PDF pp. 173-176, printed pp. 162-165,
"3.4 Factors Increasing the Working Effect of Strength," "3.4.1 The Warm-up and
Pre-Activity Preparation.")

**Why it works** — Temperature effects act at the muscle-fibre level (contraction speed and
force rise with safe-range temperature increases, and post-stimulation active-state
duration shortens with heat); the CNS-priming component works by establishing task-specific
neural readiness before the main effort, which is why "little or no general physical
warming up may be necessary" for sports (Olympic lifting, gymnastics) whose competitive
movements themselves double as adequate specific preparation, and why endurance events
(marathon) need essentially no dedicated specific warm-up since the event itself provides it.

**When to apply** — Use the Franks decision rules directly when designing warm-up protocols
by sport/session type: prescribe active, direct (task-similar), moderate-to-high-intensity
warm-ups before explosive/power/max-strength work for trained athletes specifically, and
favor lighter, indirect warm-ups (or none) before pure endurance work. **Eric's baseline:**
directly usable to formalize warm-up prescription language in Baylor's own S&C
programming and in the HHPR 5355 curriculum material, since the department's documented
practice does not currently specify a warm-up decision framework distinct from general
programming guidance.

**When NOT to apply** — The specific performance-gain numbers (jump height, punch force,
strike time) are single old studies on specific populations (women's basketball, boxers,
long jumpers) and should be treated as illustrative magnitude, not as guaranteed or
individually-applicable gains. The Franks rules are themselves a literature summary from
1983 sources, not a fresh meta-analysis; they capture broad, still-plausible patterns but
should be applied as heuristics, not fixed thresholds.

**Example** — Prescribing a long, generalized, non-specific dynamic warm-up before a
football lineman's max-effort squat testing session risks the "strenuous, non-specific
warm-up interferes with skill" failure mode per Franks; a shorter, direct (squat-pattern-specific)
warm-up ramping intensity toward the working weight better fits this framework's guidance
for trained athletes in an explosive/max-strength task.

**Related** — [[framework--post-activation-potentiation-load-timing-sequencing]] (the
immediately following subsection, on how a *specific prior strength stimulus* — not just a
general warm-up — further boosts subsequent performance).

# Atomization brief (shared by every Flint ingest agent)

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

# Eccentric Actions Produce More Force and Cost Less Energy Than Concentric, by Specific Cited Margins

**What it is** — Three related, separately-sourced findings on eccentric versus concentric
muscular work: (1) **Force**: a maximal overcoming (concentric) contraction produces
1.2-1.6x less force than the same muscle displays resisting a stretch (eccentric), per
Bethe (1929); cited examples of eccentric-over-concentric superiority are 22% for the
arms, 46.8% for the forearms, and 50% for the knee extensors. Semyonov's 1968 data on
untrained subjects gives maximal isometric knee-extensor force at 120° as 465 N versus 401
N concentric; combined-regime testing found the largest force (506 N) for slow eccentric
action following preliminary maximal isometric tension, and 453 N for eccentric following
preliminary concentric work. (2) **Energy cost**: eccentric work uses roughly half the
energy of concentric work, but only at slow movement velocities not exceeding 0.12 m/s
(Chauveau, 1904; corroborated by later work: Fenn 1924, Hartree & Hill 1928, Hill 1930,
Cattel 1983); the advantage does not extend to fast, powerful concentric-style movements.
(3) **Reflex mechanism**: the myotatic stretch reflex strengthens with the speed of the
stretch (Samoyloff & Kisseleff 1928; Foerster & Altenburg 1933; Lippold 1957), and better-trained
athletes use this reflex tension more precisely and efficiently during eccentric work
(Zakharyents, 1962). (PDF pp. 136-137, printed pp. 125-126, "3.1 Regimes of Muscular Work.")

**Why it works** — The author gives a partial mechanism for (1) and (3): the myotatic
stretch reflex adds reflexive muscular tension on top of the passive/mechanical resistance
of stretched tissue, and this stretch-driven force addition scales with stretch speed. For
(2), the text does not give a mechanistic explanation beyond citing the calorimetric/heat
studies; **Inference:** the lower metabolic cost of eccentric work is generally attributed
in modern exercise physiology to fewer cross-bridges cycling per unit of force produced
during forcible lengthening, but the book itself does not state this mechanism.

**When to apply** — Useful as a citable, quantified starting point for programming
eccentric-emphasis work (e.g. eccentric overload machines, tempo-eccentric lifting,
eccentric hamstring work) where the goal is either a large force stimulus at relatively
low metabolic/cardiovascular cost, or building the reflex-tension precision the text
associates with trained athletes. **Eric's baseline:** none of the corpus's testing or
programming documents specify eccentric-only protocols, so this is a gap this text could
inform if the department wants a citable rationale for adding eccentric-emphasis blocks.

**When NOT to apply** — All three numbers sets are single old studies (1929, 1968, 1904,
with corroborating work through 1983), largely on isolated joints or untrained subjects,
not independently re-validated within this ingest; treat the specific percentages (22%,
46.8%, 50%, the halved-energy figure) as illustrative orders of magnitude from that era's
methods, not as targets to program against directly. The energy-saving finding explicitly
does not apply above 0.12 m/s, so it cannot be used to justify eccentric training as
"more efficient" for fast, powerful, sport-relevant velocities.

**Example** — A coach citing "eccentric strength exceeds concentric by up to 50%" for
knee extensors should attribute it to Bethe (1929)/Semyonov (1968) specifically and note
it as a single-era estimate for that joint, not a universal strength-training constant.

**Related** — [[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] (the elastic-energy
storage mechanism eccentric loading exploits); [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]]
(the same stretch-speed-dependent reflex potentiation, applied to plyometric training).

# The Gap Between Absolute Strength and Achieved Force Widens as External Resistance Drops

**What it is** — Table 3.1 (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) quantifies how the "strength
deficit" — the gap between absolute strength (So) and the maximum dynamic force actually
achieved (Fmax) — changes with load: at 80% of So resistance, Fmax reaches 94.0% of So (a
6.0-point deficit, Fmax:So correlation 0.822); at 60%, Fmax reaches 82.7% (17.3-point
deficit, correlation 0.798); at 40%, Fmax reaches 64.4% (35.6-point deficit, correlation
0.657); at 20%, Fmax reaches only 47.7% (52.3-point deficit, correlation 0.316). In other
words, the lighter the load relative to an athlete's absolute strength, the smaller the
fraction of that absolute strength they actually realize, and the weaker the statistical
link between how strong someone tests (So) and how much force they produce in that lighter,
faster movement. (PDF p. 141, printed p. 130, "3.2.1 Explosive Strength," Table 3.1, Figs
3.3-3.4.)

**Why it works** — The curves for different loads are described as "precisely superimposed
upon each other at their beginning" (early F(t) curve, Fig 3.4) regardless of load, which
the author attributes to starting-strength being a resistance-independent neuromuscular
ability; as the movement continues past that initial shared segment, higher loads allow
more time for force to keep building toward So before the limb finishes accelerating,
while light loads are already moving (and thus limiting further force production) before
peak force is reached — hence the growing deficit at lower resistance.

**When to apply** — Use as a citable, quantified rationale for why maximal-strength testing
(1RM, isometric mid-thigh pull) does not directly predict performance in light, fast tasks,
and why light-load/unloaded-movement testing and heavy-load testing measure increasingly
different things as load drops. **Eric's baseline:** this directly supports the department's
existing testing-battery design logic of using multiple load conditions rather than a
single strength number — e.g., pairing 1RM/isometric strength testing with CMJ and sprint
testing (`method-baseline.md`, "Testing and assessment"; force-plate CMJ family per
`revised-force-plate-testing-v3.md`) — because this table gives the quantitative reason
a single heavy-load strength number correlates poorly (R=0.316 at 20% load) with light,
fast output.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999) built from a
specific leg-press-style task; the four discrete resistance points (80/60/40/20% of So) are
not a continuous, generally-validated curve, and the exact correlation coefficients should
not be extrapolated to other joints, exercises, or populations without re-testing. It also
does not by itself tell a coach what to train — it describes the relationship, not a
training prescription.

**Example** — An athlete with an elite back-squat 1RM but an average CMJ is not necessarily
undertrained; per this table, low-load output (like an unloaded jump, effectively near the
0% end of this curve) is only weakly tied to absolute strength, so the more informative
diagnostic is a light-to-moderate-load force-velocity profile, not the 1RM alone.

**Related** — [[framework--strength-deficit-jump-comparison-estimate]] (Ch1, the SJ-vs-CMJ
field proxy for the same Fmax-vs-Fmm strength-deficit concept, which this table's PDF-page
citation explicitly points forward to); [[framework--four-component-model-of-explosive-force]]
(the four-ability decomposition underlying this same F(t) dataset).

# The Reactivity Coefficient (RC) and Verkhoshansky's Depth-Jump Reactivity Test

**What it is** — Reactive ability (the neuromuscular capacity to generate explosive force
via a preliminary stretch immediately before concentric work) is quantified with a
**Reactivity Coefficient**: the lab-only form RC = K2/K1 (a ratio of two characteristics
of muscular work, e.g. power, before and after the stretch), and the field-practical form
**RC = Fmax / (tmax x m x g)**, where Fmax is peak force, tmax is time to reach it, m is
the moving mass (or bodymass), and g is gravitational acceleration. Verkhoshansky's own
"reactivity test" protocol: a series of vertical jumps without arm-swing, performed after
a depth-jump from 0.4 m, unloaded and then with 10, 20, 30, and 40 kg added; jump height
and support-period duration are recorded and plotted against added mass. Findings from this
protocol: reactive ability correlates with strength most strongly at large loads (R = 0.95
at 30-40 kg loads, weak at lighter loads); RC correlates more strongly with support-period
time than with force in every load condition; absolute strength has a *negative* effect on
contraction speed with small/no added load but a *positive* effect with large added load
(40 kg), while high *relative* strength has the opposite pattern (positive with light
loads, negative with heavy loads); and cross-sport testing (Fig 3.9-3.10) found jumpers
had the highest RC and middle-distance runners the lowest, with RC showing a strong linear
relationship (R ≈ 0.95) to triple-jump performance specifically. (PDF pp. 146-149, printed
pp. 135-138, "Quickness and Reactive Ability," Figs 3.7-3.10.)

**Why it works** — The author's mechanism: a preliminary stretch elastically deforms the
muscle-tendon complex, storing potential energy that converts to kinetic energy on the
subsequent contraction, adding to active muscular force; RC operationalizes "how much of
that stored-energy advantage shows up, relative to how much time and body/load mass it
took to produce peak force," which is why it tracks support-period time more tightly than
raw force output.

plyometric-prescription framework by itself — it measures reactive ability, it does not
prescribe how to train it (see [[framework--shock-method-and-plyometric-terminology]] for
that).

Verkhoshansky's data implies the athlete whose reactive ability holds up (or improves) as
external load increases from 0 to 40 kg is a different training case than one whose
reactive ability only shows up unloaded — the former likely has more absolute strength to
draw on, the latter is leaning more on relative strength/elasticity.

# Peak Power Load Is Very Different in the Lab (~25% Max) vs a Real Competition Lift (~65-70% Max)

**What it is** — In simple isotonic muscle-contraction models, power (P = F x V) peaks at
roughly one-third of maximal contraction speed and one-quarter of maximal force — i.e.
maximal isotonic power is displayed against a load requiring about 25% of the muscle's
maximal force (Wilkie, 1950). But the text explicitly warns this laboratory pattern "can
differ significantly" from functional, multi-joint activities: in the competitive
powerlifting squat, peak power for a group of elite (+125 kg class) lifters (mean best
squat 407.4 kg) occurred at a load of about **280 kg — roughly two-thirds of their maximum**
— producing 1451 watts over 0.85 seconds; power dropped to 52% of that peak at true maximal
load, and time-to-complete-the-lift increased by 282% from the peak-power load to the
maximal load (Fig 3.17). (PDF pp. 157-158, printed pp. 146-147, "3.3.2 The Effect of the
Load on Speed of Muscle Contraction," Fig 3.17.)

**Why it works** — The author gives no separate mechanism beyond noting the mismatch
between idealized single-muscle isotonic models and the real biomechanics of a
multi-joint, whole-body competition lift; **Inference:** a full competition squat recruits
many muscle groups and joints with different individual force-velocity properties,
technique constraints, and stability demands that a single-muscle isotonic model cannot
capture, which likely shifts the practical power-peak load well above the single-muscle
theoretical prediction.

**When to apply** — Use the ~65-70%-of-1RM figure, not the classical 25%-of-max figure,
when programming loads intended to maximize power output in barbell squat-pattern lifts
specifically (this is close to modern velocity-based-training guidance for squat-pattern
power work). **Inference:** for Baylor's programming, this is a useful citable historical
data point supporting load selection in the 60-70% 1RM range for power-focused squat work,
though it should be triangulated against the department's own velocity-based methods
(Perch) rather than applied as a fixed rule, since VBT data on the specific athlete and
exercise is more direct evidence than this single 1988-era powerlifting dataset.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a single dataset from a specific competitive population
(elite super-heavyweight powerlifters) and a single exercise (the competition squat); it
should not be generalized to other lifts (e.g. Olympic lifts, ballistic movements, upper
body pressing) without separate data, and it does not override or replace the classical
25%-of-max figure for the isolated, single-joint contractions that figure was actually
derived from — the two describe different kinds of movement, not contradictory answers to
the same question.

**Example** — Programming a powerlifting-style back squat for peak power output at "25% of
1RM" (the classical isotonic-model figure) would badly undershoot the load that actually
produces peak power output in the real lift, per this dataset's ~65-70% figure.

**Related** — [[claim--force-velocity-curve-limitations-and-in-vivo-deviations]] (the
broader caution about applying single-muscle force-velocity models to real, multi-joint
tasks that this finding exemplifies).
